items.title: European diplomats attacked by Israeli settlers in West Bank
items.summary: The Israeli military condemns the violence but the prime minister's office says it is part of a "smear" campaign.
items.content:
Image caption, Masked settlers are accused of attacking the convoy
Diplomatic correspondent ,Â  Reporting from Jerusalem
A delegation of European diplomats has been attacked by masked Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank.
Belgium condemned the assault on its consul general and the other envoys, while France decried the attack as "appalling". Both called for Israel to bring those responsible to justice.
The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) also condemned what they called "the severe act of violence" and said they were investigating.
But the office of the Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu cast doubt on what happened, suggesting it was part of a "co-ordinated campaign to smear Israel".
The attack came only a day after a number of Palestinians and Heidi Levine, a Washington Post photographer, were injured in a separate assault by settlers in another village in the West Bank.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the attack on Levine was "disturbing" and "not a good look".
It was also condemned by the US ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, who called it a "despicable act of terror carried out by masked cowards". A staunch ally of Israel, Huckabee said the assailants must face "prosecution to the fullest extent of the law".
Figure caption, Rubio 'very disturbed' over video of West Bank settler attack on US journalist
In Saturday's incident, the European diplomats - from Belgium, France, Poland and the Catholic Church - had come to the largely Christian village of Taybeh near Ramallah.
They were there to assess the situation on the ground after almost near daily attacks by Israeli settlers on Palestinians trying to bring in their olive harvest.
Video footage from the scene showed masked settlers confronting the convoy. Reports suggest stones were thrown.
The Belgian authorities said a car from its consulate had a window smashed and a French mayor was assaulted. Video showed a man wearing a French tricolor sash slumped beside a vehicle.
Belgium's foreign minister Maxime Prevot condemned the attack and said Israel had a responsibility to bring those responsible to justice, as well as ensuring the safety of diplomats, journalists and Palestinians.
"Palestinians face this violence every day. Settlers also target journalists reporting on it and diplomats. Harvesting olives, reporting the news or carrying out diplomatic duties should never put anyone at risk of attack," he said.
He also said Belgium will continue to press for EU sanctions against those responsible for the violence.
Image caption, Palestinians have been harvesting olives in the West Bank this week before Israeli settlers attack
France's Foreign Minister Jean-NoÃ«l Barrot echoed those sentiments, calling on Israeli authorities to "urgently halt this criminal violence and guarantee the safety of civilian populations".
Poland's foreign affairs ministry also called for a "firm response" from Israeli authorities and for "an end to the spiral of violence in the West Bank".
The EU condemned the attacks, urged Israel to abide by international and human rights law, and end the expansion of settlements.
A spokesperson said that while they acknowledged some Israeli officials had condemned the attacks, they said they still expect "full accountability as well as effective measures" to stop the continued violence against Palestinians and journalists.
Gideon Sa'ar, Israel's foreign minister, said he strongly condemned the violence by what he called "Israeli rioters". He said the foreign ministry was in contact with the ambassadors of the countries involved.
But he added: "Without detracting from the severity of the incident, it is unfortunate that the visit was not coordinated with the IDF in advance. Such coordination could have helped safeguard the visitors' security."
The IDF said they "strongly condemn the severe act of violence that took place in the area of Taybeh, during which diplomatic representatives were attacked by Israeli rioters."
"According to a preliminary inquiry, no IDF soldiers were present at the scene at the time of the attack," they added.
Image caption, Netanyahu's office named the injured French official as Bernard Baudoux, the left-wing mayor of Aulnoye-Aymeries
But Netanyahu's office urged "caution before drawing conclusions" from reports about the attack.
It said the images on social media "do not establish the complete sequence of events or individual responsibility".
A statement continued: "Those circumstances remain under investigation. Israeli police and forensic investigators have launched an investigation to establish the facts and identify those responsible."
It added that "these reports come amid concerns about a coordinated campaign to smear Israel and the Jewish residents of Judea and Samaria during the annual olive harvest, relying on sensational headlines before the full facts emerge".
Netanyahu's office named the injured French official as Bernard Baudoux. The left-wing mayor of Aulnoye-Aymeries in northern France told the AFP news agency the attack showed a tolerance by Israel's right-wing government for settler violence.
The mayor said the settlers kicked him and beat him with iron bars, throwing him to the ground.
"It's the gratuitous nature of the violence that stuns me," he said. "They arrived completely enraged."
"The whole world needs to know what's happening there. For me, I'll go back to my country and everything will be fine. Those who continue to suffer the most are those who are here," he said.

items.title: 'You are the real target': Netanyahu warns Iran developing ICBMs, nuclear weapons to target US - The Jerusalem Post
items.summary: 'You are the real target': Netanyahu warns Iran developing ICBMs, nuclear weapons to target US  The Jerusalem Post
items.content:
'You are the real target': Netanyahu warns Iran developing ICBMs, nuclear weapons to target US
Netanyahu told FOX News that, if reelected prime minister, his key objectives would be to end the threat posed by Iran, expand the Abraham Accords, and seize the future of AI development.
Prime Minister and Likud party chairman Benjamin Netanyahu visits supporters in the northern Israeli city of Haifa, ahead of Israel’s upcoming general elections, October 14, 2026
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu warned that Iran was developing intercontinental ballistic missiles and pursuing nuclear weapons with the aim of threatening American cities, telling FOX News on Saturday that the US, rather than Israel, was the Iranian regime's ultimate target.
Netanyahu argued that Iran's ambitions extend beyond Israel, warning that the regime intends to target both the US and Europe if it succeeds in destroying Israel. He said Iran's development of long-range missiles and pursuit of a nuclear arsenal were intended to place American cities at the mercy of the regime.
"They understand that if they can destroy Israel, then they can conquer the Middle East, control the waterways of the world... and then proceed to the next target, which is you. That's why they're building intercontinental missiles: to reach the United States," Netanyahu said.
"This is a regime that chants death to Israel, death to America. You are the real target. And I think we are well on our way to achieving this, with President Trump's brilliant leadership, both military and, then, economic blockade."
The prime minister explained that the Iranian regime views the US as "the great Satan" and Israel as the "little Satan," before directing a remark at European countries.
A Ghadr 1 class Shahab 3 long range missile is prepared for launch during a test from an unknown location in central Iran (credit: REUTERS)
He said he "hoped our European friends are not offended; you are seen as the middle-sized Satan, you are mediocre in so many ways."
"Iran would be a nuclear power as we've never seen in the entire world, because they don't have this careful calculus of cause and benefit. Because they are so fanatic. So you can't win them over, you can't buy them out," he said.
Netanyahu also described the Iranian regime as a "malevolent power" operating alongside what he called the "Three Hs": Hamas, Hezbollah, and the Houthis.
"They are the arms of this toxic octopus. And it's not Iranian people; they are great people," he added.
Eliminating the Iranian threat was the first of three priorities Netanyahu outlined for his next term if reelected in the October 27 Knesset election, alongside expanding the Abraham Accords and establishing Israel as a global leader in artificial intelligence.
"First, we will achieve the complete elimination of the Iranian threat to Israel, to America, and to the entire world," Netanyahu said.
"Second thing is to expand the historic Abraham Accords that [US President Donald] Trump and I forged here with four Arab states," Netanyahu continued.
"There are many more that are waiting in this precise moment, because they saw our strength, our power and fortitude. And they want to join us. So let's create an axis of peace and moderation against these barbarians who shoot their own people," he said.
Netanyahu also said he plans to "forge a different future, a different Middle East, and also a different world" if reelected.
Prime Minister and Likud party chairman Benjamin Netanyahu visits supporters in the northern Israeli city of Haifa, ahead of Israel’s upcoming general elections, October 14, 2026. (credit: Sharon Leibel/Flash90)
Netanyahu's third priority focused on artificial intelligence, and the prime minister said he agreed with Trump on both the dangers the technology poses and its potential benefits for humanity.
"I plan to seize the future with the 'Neverland AI,' the 'super intelligence,' as the president calls it. He is absolutely right; they are dangerous, but their possibilities in health, in agriculture, in transport, and in education ," he explained.
"You can personalize AI for every child; they have their own potential, and you can give them the best teachers on the planet. We are doing it today in Israel, and we intend to be the world leaders in that area too. These are all amazing things," he added.
Netanyahu also pointed to Israel's economic performance, which he described as among the strongest in the developed world.
"By the way, the economy, according to the International Monetary Fund (IMF), is leading all the Western countries, the OCD countries, with the greatest growth. That's after three years of war. I want to push that even further, bring a better future to Israel, to our neighbors, to our great ally the United States."

items.title: US, Israel face threats of war if oil prices keep rising - The Jerusalem Post
items.summary: US, Israel face threats of war if oil prices keep rising  The Jerusalem Post
items.content:
Oil prices over $100 could affect war with Iran, leading to escalation before elections - analysis
The US and Israel know that the main hurdle to keeping the lid on the war with Iran is the price of oil, and it will keep rising if no solution can be found for Hormuz and the Houthis.
Vessels transit the Strait of Hormuz off the coast of the port city of Bandar Abbas in southern Iran on September 5, 2026; illustrative
( photo credit : ATTA KENARE / AFP via Getty Images )
High oil prices are going to be an issue over the next few weeks if they continue to stay above $100 a barrel. That is a clear challenge for the United States and also potentially for Israel in terms of keeping a lid on a renewed conflict with Iran prior to the elections in both countries.
It is no secret that the looming elections have tended to change dynamics, estimations, and assessments about whether the conflict could start again.
The high oil prices come during a decline in stock prices on Wall Street. This is amid concerns about AI companies and energy prices. That could tend to be a kind of triple threat affecting the US, and thus also affecting Israel.
There has been a lot of messaging about how the Strait of Hormuz is open and the availability of alternative energy sources, but the question is whether or not the global market will accept these assertions.
Recent videos show ships sinking in the Strait of Hormuz and all sorts of containers floating away as ships are in distress. This is not something that will boost global optimism regarding supply chains, and it always remains a question whether enough ships are transporting energy supplies.
Flames burn at a facility belonging to Saudi oil giant Aramco south of Riyadh on October 3, 2026. (credit: AFP VIA GETTY IMAGES)
It also leads to questions about what the Houthis might do. The Houthis could try to threaten the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. They could also encourage other Iranian proxies, such as those in Iraq, to continue attacks on Saudi oil and gas energy infrastructure.
A mysterious explosion in Iraq on Saturday appears to have struck an Iranian proxy group. All this could continue to disrupt global trade.
When there are attacks on pipelines or transit points in Saudi Arabia, for instance, it takes weeks to repair them. That creates disruption, and all those disruptions add up to the feeling in the global market that there is too much uncertainty.
This kind of uncertainty will affect the US. It already appears to be affecting US policy regarding the Ukraine war and Russia, and this is the kind of thing that can lead to escalation in the Middle East or miscalculations in which something happens again with Iran.
Iran continues to be blockaded , but it also tends to feel a bit confident about its next steps. Therefore, we are seeing a potential for escalation within the next week or two.
Iran also knows there are elections in Israel and the US; therefore, Iran and its proxies may want to take advantage of this period.

Share Russia’s war on Ukraine ‘must be brought to an end’, Zelenskyy says on social media
Volodymyr Zelenskyy at a European Union summit in Brussels on Friday [Yves Herman/Reuters]
Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said that the war with Russia “must be brought to an end” and that his country is preparing for the “next steps” of diplomacy to end the conflict.
Zelenskyy said on X on Sunday that he had a “conversation with the American president’s envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner”. He added that “a lot depends” on the US position, but it’s clear there are “many things that matter to all of us”.

The Ukrainian leader’s comments come amid a significant diplomatic fallout with US President Donald Trump, who on Saturday waived expected sanctions targeting Russia’s energy economy and previously called renewed Ukrainian strikes on Russian energy infrastructure “a disgrace”.
Nonetheless, Zelenskyy said his team is in “virtually nonstop communication” with their US counterparts and said a focus of dialogue is on the results of the talks in Florida and further steps.
Also on Sunday, Zelenskyy said he was “thankful” that the US had resumed intelligence sharing with Ukraine after a pause left Ukraine particularly vulnerable to Russia’s regular ballistic missile attacks.
“It was blocked for some period of time. And then it was deblocked by the American side,” Zelenskyy told NBC, adding: “Only [the] United States has this unique intelligence to tell our side when Russia uses ballistic missiles. And we didn’t get it during ballistic attacks during three days”.
Kyiv has also reported restrictions on the speed of satellite service Starshield, a military-grade version of Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite connectivity network, provided to Ukraine by Musk’s company SpaceX.
Ukraine said its relays were experiencing a limit on how fast receivers could travel while maintaining connectivity, making it almost impossible to intercept Russia’s upgraded jet-powered long-range drones.
Musk had said any restrictions imposed on Starshield connectivity were the responsibility of the US government. The White House quickly rebuked that and in an NBC interview on Sunday, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent called Zelenskyy “very reckless” for accusing the US of throttling connectivity.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Sunday that Ukraine is currently blocked from Starshield, and that a request from Kyiv to access the system for attacks deep inside Russia is “under discussion”.
Also on Sunday, Ukrainian media reported that Russian strikes killed two people in the western Volyn region, near the border with Poland, and injured at least five others across the country. Overnight attacks by Russia killed a woman and injured a six-year-old in the Zaporizhzhia region.
On Saturday night and in the early hours of Sunday, Ukraine hit Russia’s second-largest city, St Petersburg , with a significant drone attack. It targeted a key oil refinery and depot, a warehouse of Russian online retailer Ozon and a data centre run by Russian social media company, VKontakte.
At least one person was killed in the attack, which Russian state media said was the largest on the city since the start of the war in 2022.

items.title: Macron calls for calm in France and warns rioting must not escalate
items.summary: French President Emmanuel Macron made a national television address after rioting caused widespread damage.
items.content:
Image caption, French President Macron (centre) chaired an inter-ministerial crisis meeting at the ÃlysÃ©e Presidential Palace, in Paris, on Sunday
French President Emmanuel Macron has called for "calm and order" after a major day of protests turned into rioting and looting on Saturday, and as some disorder continued in Paris on Sunday.
In a national address from the ÃlysÃ©e Palace, he warned those who had taken part not to "escalate", adding: "We all feel anger and shame."
Some 550,000 demonstrators took to the streets for largely peaceful protests against rising fuel prices, the cost of living and deteriorating public services, including schools.
Macron said a distinction must be drawn between the "legitimate demands" of protesters and "those who destroyed, smashed and looted".
Police have arrested about 2,400 people, according to France's interior ministry.
The French president said "nothing justifies" the "unbridled" violence seen and said those involved would face justice.
Groups of rioters, some dressed in black and wearing masks and balaclavas, also came out in Paris, Marseille and other towns and cities, with some setting fire to cars and buildings.
On Sunday, looting and clashes with police continued on a smaller scale in parts of the capital and Lyon.
Tear gas and stun grenades were fired at hundreds of people in Paris, according to the AFP news agency, and bottles and rocks were again hurled at police.
Image caption, Local officials said the Limoges town hall was "largely lost" after fire caused part of the building to collapse
Sunday saw cities across the country confront the impact of what developed into one of the worst bouts of disorder in modern French history.
In Limoges, the ornate 19th Century city hall was gutted by a fire started by rioters on Saturday, its clock tower and roof collapsing and the flames took hold.
Speaking near the ruined building, AnnÃ¨yse said: "This is very upsetting. Harming heritage buildings just because you are angry at the government is selfish, I think. It's hurting everybody."
"It's awful and unbelievable," said another man who gave his name as Gerrard. "We are very sad and I think it will be a long time to put it back as it was before."
Shopkeepers were seen early on Sunday morning picking up large shards of glass in Paris as rubbish trucks cleared up debris on some of the larger streets.
Figure caption, Watch: James Waterhouse speaks to looted shop owvers on the streets of Paris
Widespread looting took place across the cities of Paris, Marseille and Lille, as well as other areas.
Macron said local prefects and mayors would draft measures to protections in place for shops and civic buildings.
The president also said there would be "full transparency" over the police response to the demonstrations.
Tear gas and water cannon were turned on crowds over the weekend and riot police were seen hitting people with batons in several places.
France's interior ministry said about 1,000 police officers were injured on Saturday, seven of them seriously.

The UKMTO reported an increase of attacks on vessels in the Strait of Hormuz [Fatemeh Bahrami/Getty Images]
Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) has said two oil tankers, each carrying about two million barrels of crude oil, caught fire after hitting naval mines in the Strait of Hormuz.
The first tanker hit a mine, triggering an explosion and a “fierce fire”, the IRGC said on Saturday, while the second tanker hit a mine that engulfed it “in a massive blaze”, Iran’s official IRNA news agency reported.

list 2 of 3 US-Iran stalemate: What are Trump’s next military options?

Information about the ships’ names or the origin of their cargo was not immediately available.
IRNA said the vessels had switched off their positioning and radar systems and tried to use a route not authorised by Iran.
The IRGC also claimed that while one tanker tried to cross the waterway “with US support”, the second vessel was left immobilised.
Iran seized control of the Strait of Hormuz after the US-Israeli war on the country began in late February. Tehran has since demanded that all ships seek its authorisation before transiting. About one-fifth of global oil consumption transited the waterway before the war.
This week, IRGC naval commander Rear Admiral Ali Azmaei warned that any vessel that deactivated its navigation systems would be considered “hostile”.
The United States has imposed its own naval counter-blockade on Iranian oil exports.
Iran’s army earlier said that two tankers caught fire on Thursday and Friday in Tehran’s “prohibited zone” in the Gulf of Oman.
Maritime monitors also reported two tankers struck in Gulf waters off Saudi Arabia on Friday.
Last Sunday, six vessels were attacked in or near the Strait of Hormuz, the most in a single day since the war began, according to security firm Vanguard, the International Maritime Organization and the UK maritime agency UKMTO.
Attacks around the waterway have surged over the past two weeks, with Iran saying it is stepping up strikes in response to the US blockade of its ports and tougher sanctions imposed last month.
Nearly 20.8 million barrels of oil passed through on October 8, but only 2.9 million on October 11, according to Kpler data.
The disruption has pushed up global energy prices and inflation.
US President Donald Trump has explicitly ruled out using a nuclear weapon against Iran. “I wouldn’t use nuclear,” he told the Newsmax news site in an interview on Thursday.
Trump said that he was also not considering putting troops on the ground in Iran. “No, I don’t see that, I don’t see it,” he said, adding he believes a deal to end the war will be reached after the November 3 US midterm elections.

items.summary: Interior minister says ‘the Republic will not yield’ to France’s worst protests in yearsA dispatch here from Sam Jones, our reporter in Madrid, as protests have spread to Italy and PortugalThe angry protests that have convulsed Spain and France in recent weeks have spilled over to Italy and Portugal, with rioters clashing with police and setting property on fire in Milan, and a tent encampment springing up
items.content:
Arrests over France protests rise to 1,800, with whole streets in Paris ‘devastated’ – Europe live
Interior minister says ‘the Republic will not yield’ to France’s worst protests in years
Sun 18 Oct 2026 10.50 EDT First published on Sun 18 Oct 2026 03.48 EDT
Trump says "France is burning" as he blames violence on immigration
Police clash with students and workers protesting in Paris – video
Trump says "France is burning" as he blames violence on immigration
It’s approaching 5pm in Paris, as we await French President Emmanuel Macron’s televised response to large-scale protests and unrest across France on Saturday.
Macron will address the French public on TV at 8pm (7pm BST) after crisis meetings with ministers on Sunday.
France’s interior minister Laurent Nunez said “the Republic will not yield” after 1,800 were arrested across the country on Saturday.
Protests which had begun about education and schooling conditions in France have broadened to wider cost of living issues.
Buildings were set alight, including Limoges City Hall in central France, as other cities suffered widespread vandalism.
More than 500 police officers, gendarmes and firefighters were injured.
Nunez blamed thousands of “far left” protesters along with criminals who “looted and ransacked” buildings.
The numbers of protesters on Saturday have varied, with authorities saying 550,000 took to the streets nationwide, but organisers said it was about 800,000.
Paris police said 110,000 took part in a march. Sunday has not seen similar incidents.
The cost of damage to shops will run to hundreds of millions of euros, according to the president of a trade body.
US president Donald Trump said “France is burning” and blamed immigration in a post on Truth Social.
Other protests took place against the cost of living in Spain, Italy and Portugal.
Our Paris correspondent Angelique Chrisafis has this dispatch from France , ahead of Emmanuel Macron’s address to the nation on Sunday night.
The French government was in crisis talks on Sunday after one of the most violent days of unrest in years left public buildings burned, hundreds of shops destroyed and looted and more than 2000 people arrested in cities across the country.
Politicians on the left and far-right called for the resignation of the interior minister, Laurent Nunez after the government appeared to have been caught by surprise by the scale of violence. State buildings were stormed and torched, bus-stops smashed, roads barricaded and shops broken into and destroyed.
The president Emmanuel Macron , who is standing down next spring as the far-right Marine Le Pen polls high for the presidential election, was preparing to address the nation on Sunday night.
He wrote on social media there was “no place for violence” in France.
Police and officials faced challenges of different types on Saturday.
First, tens of thousands of peaceful protestors attended calm marches through major cities including Paris, supporting schoolchildren’s demands for more teachers and repairs to decrepit schools .
Those marches, which came after four weeks of street marches and barricades of schools , were attended by parents, teachers and grandparents as well as students and workers protesting over the high cost of living.
The demonstrators carried banners saying the government was not listening to them and calling for more money for public services.
But separately to those peaceful demonstrations, different groups caught police and officials by surprise with moving gatherings, sporadic burning, barricading streets and clashing with police in different parts of cities including Paris , Bordeaux, Nice and Marseille.
Finally, masked looters took advantage of what French media called the “chaos” on the streets to smash shopfronts and grab goods.
If you’re just catching up on the demonstrations across Europe which turned violent on Saturday, this is why some of them are happening.
Why are people taking to the streets across Europe?
People have been protesting in countries across Europe, including Spain, France and Portugal over their unhappiness at the state of schools and wider cost of living crisis.
In France , the activism has largely been led by high school pupils who have clashed with police in often violent protests over long hours, missing teachers, dilapidated classrooms and an opaque university admissions system. Pupils routinely miss months of teaching due to unfilled staff absences.
Other demonstrators have then joined student marches to voice their unhappiness about rising living costs, including over fuel prices after US bombing caused the effective closure of the strait of Hormuz.
The General Confederation of Labour (CGT), one of France’s largest unions, has backed the protests and called for lower prices, higher pensions and boosted wages.
French president Emmanual Macron is nearing the end of his time in the Élysée Palace after serving two terms.
Over the Pyrenees in Spain activists took to the streets in September over housing prices.
They were triggered by the eviction of a 87-year-old woman from her home after an investment fund hiked her rent by 230%. María del Carmen Abascal died a fortnight later after being admitted to hospital.
Protesters have called for lower rents, an end to evictions and a ban on investment funds buying property.
Similar pleas were made across the Iberian border in Portugal on Saturday, with hundreds gathering in central Lisbon.
Portuguese housing prices rose by 124% between 2015 and 2024, roughly twice as fast as the EU average, according to official data.
Squeezed household budgets were also at the centre of marches in Milan, Italy .
A march on Saturday began peacefully but ended with masked rioters throwing stones, paving blocks and other objects at riot police and setting fire to barricades made from bar tables.
Meanwhile student-protests in Albania against the prime minister, Edi Rama, entered their sixth day on Sunday.
Demonstrators have said they are unhappy with perceived corruption , a lack of jobs and poor education standards.
The education protests in France began in late September, week after the start of the school year.
However demonstrations have since intensified, reaching the high point on Saturday.
Saturday was also the first day of cost of living protests in Italy, Portugal and Belgium.
In Albania protests have been taking place since the summer, triggered by a luxury coastal development backed by Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner.
In France the government has said it would deploy 3,000 more substitute teachers to deal with shortages, and said it would include students in decision-making for schools.
It also scrapped plans to increase some university registration fees, which it had announced for next year’s budget.
Fuel protests in mid-September led to an announcement by the Elysee that the government would increase petrol subsidies for certain industries.
Spain’s president Pedro Sánchez attempted to pass emergency housing legislation that would have protected tenants in the rental market.
The Socialist party leader’s defeat led him to calling an early election for 29 November , as he told the public he needed a “broader progressive majority” to get the new laws through.
Macron will give a televised address on Sunday night after holding a crisis meeting with key ministers.
His interior minister Laurent Nunez appeared to signal the French government are not willing to concede further, as he blamed “far left” protesters and “criminals who looted and ransacked” buildings across France.
If Sanchez wins the Spanish election in November, and is able to pass the emergency housing legislation that was stymied last month, then it could see marches in Spain end.
The US president Donald Trump said “France is burning” and the country has been “shattered” by immigration in a post on Truth Social.
He said: “France is burning! The immigration of people from an entirely different world, people with hatred in their hearts, has shattered that once-great country. Close your borders and take control before it is too late!”
French authorities and police have not linked immigrants to the rioting and have repeatedly attributed some of the violence to “radical far-left groups” and other people who joined to loot.
Trump’s post comes after similar comments made by vice president JD Vance on Saturday.
“Western liberals imported the third world into France and other countries in the name of diversity and compassion. They ignored fundamental questions of assimilation and compatibility. They were told it would lead to this and they didn’t listen,” Vance wrote on X.
“I pray that France, a beautiful country of amazing people, will stop this madness before more of its landmarks burn,” he added.
Elsewhere in Europe , violent protests are also continuing Albania, where thousands have been calling for the prime minister to step down as they rally against poor university conditions, high tuition fees and corruption.
Albanian’s capital saw protests on Sunday for a sixth day in a row as the prime minister, Edi Rama, ruled out resigning, the main demand of the protesters.
Hundreds of protesters gathered again in Tirana on Sunday at noon in front of the education ministry chanting “Rama, resign” in a tense standoff with the police, who later used water cannons and tear gas to hold back the crowds.
A protester prepares to throw a petrol bomb toward riot police during clashes at an anti-government demonstration in Tirana, Albania. Photograph: Hameraldi Agolli/AP Shops and institutions in the centre of the city have secured their doors and windows with metal shutters, while city workers removed paving stones to prevent their use by protesters.
In an over-an-hour long video broadcast earlier in the day, Rama ruled out resigning, stating that the protests are the “work of an outside hand”.
Writer and activist Lura Elezi, 38, told AFP that she is protesting for “a better life, rule of law and against crime and corruption”.
“I love my country, but my government does not respect us - it defies us. Every citizen must take responsibility for their country, taking on the duty to lead, to love, and not to destroy one’s own nation,” she said.
Tirana saw its harshest violence on Saturday when protesters threw rocks, Molotov cocktails, metal objects and pyrotechnic devices at police, and torched cars and litter bins, using them as blazing barricades to stop police advancing.
A protester throws a cobblestone during an anti-government demonstration in central Tirana Saturday Photograph: Armend Nimani/AFP/Getty Images The morning newspapers after the night before, here’s how the French press covered Saturday’s protests on Sunday morning.
Le Parisien Dimanche captured the scenes in the Capital with protests taking place near the Monument à la République.
Le Parisien Dimanche on 18 October Photograph: frontpages.com Left leaning newspaper Libération went with “Giving a voice to students”, referring to the genesis of the protests.
Libération on 18 October. Photograph: frontpages.com The financial Sunday newspaper La Tribune Dimanche’s front page was headlined “Six months until the Presidential election: Chaos”, again showing the scenes near the Monument à la République.
La Tribune Dimanche on 18 October Photograph: frontpages.com The centre-right newspaper Le Figaro referred to a “a month of blockades and destruction”.
Le Figaro on 18 October. Photograph: frontpages.com Meanwhile France’s widest-read paid national daily newspaper Le Monde details how Macron “lost the youth”, referring to the protests.
Le Monde on 18 October. Photograph: frontpages.com French President Emmanuel Macron will hold a crisis meeting with ministers on Sunday before he addresses the public, Agence France Presse reports.
Macron will sit down with members of his cabinet on Sunday, the Elysee has said, ahead of his televised speech to the French public this evening.
It was to come as France counts the cost of Saturday’s protests, which saw clashes, arson and widespread looting.
Ministers have blamed “ultra-left” groups for the violence, which erupted six months before the French go to the polls to elect Macron’s successor.
Interior minister Laurent Nunez said thousands of “far-left” protesters had been joined by “criminals who looted and ransacked” buildings across France.
A dispatch here from Sam Jones, our reporter in Madrid, as protests have spread to Italy and Portugal
The angry protests that have convulsed Spain and France in recent weeks have spilled over to Italy and Portugal , with rioters clashing with police and setting property on fire in Milan, and a tent encampment springing up in Lisbon over the weekend.
A march in central Milan on Saturday to protest against rising living costs began peacefully but ended with masked rioters throwing stones, paving blocks and other objects at riot police and setting fire to barricades made from bar tables.
Police used water cannon and teargas to disperse the crowds, and images of the aftermath showed a severely damaged carabinieri car.
At least two police officers were injured and about 50 demonstrators, including many minors, were detained, the LaPresse news agency reported.
Italy’s prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, said that while demonstrating was a right, “setting our cities ablaze is not”. In a social media post, she said “hooligans” had exploited the protests “to sow chaos, attack those responsible for ensuring security and to hold entire cities hostage”.
‘We are suffocating’: protests spread to Lisbon and Milan as housing and living cost tensions intensify
Emmanuel Macron will give a televised address to the French public this evening on the protests and unrest on Saturday.
The French President will speak at 8pm French time (6pm GMT), after more than 1,800 people were arrested on Saturday in connection with violence that spread from protests against the cost of living.
Paris police said about 110,000 people took part in a protest march on Saturday against the cost of living and school conditions.
Numbers have differed for those nationwide, with authorities saying it was about 550,000 but organisers claiming it was higher at about 800,000.
One person died of a heart attack, Paris police said. French media reported a protester suffered a medical emergency in the street during the march.
Thirteen police and gendarmerie officers and two firefighters were injured, the statement said, according to Associated Press.
The mayors of France’s three largest cities, Paris, Marseille and Lyon have requested a meeting with the prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, in the coming days.
Around Paris’ Place de la République on Sunday morning, dislodged cobblestones, shattered storefronts and broken glass marked the aftermath of the events.
Looting and damage were reported around the square and in some other tourist and shopping areas in the city centre.
Police said groups numbering from several hundred to more than 1,000 people formed unauthorised marches across central Paris on Saturday.
“By late afternoon, a new phase began with the arrival of large numbers of people whose sole aim was to steal and loot, taking advantage of the unrest,” police said.
Protests in France caused damage worth hundreds of millions of euros, according to the head of a trade body representing shop owners.
About 1,500 shops and retailers were damaged in the demonstrations according to Alexandre Bompard, president of the Retail and Trade Federation.
He told LCI television the cost to the establishments will run to “several hundreds of millions of euros”.
More than 1,800 people have been arrested in France over protests on Saturday, the country’s interior minister Laurent Nunez has said.
Nunez, in a post on X, said “the Republic will not yield” as more than 500 police officers, gendarmes and firefighters have been injured in the demonstrations.
“The material damage is considerable,” Nunez added, pointing to damaged shops.
He blamed thousands of “far-left” protesters along with “criminals who looted and ransacked” buildings across France.
“The Republic will yield nothing to those who seek to impose disorder and violence,” he said.
Causing disorder through violence and in a coordinated manner is not.
Attacking our law enforcement officers, targeting our institutions, damaging public buildings, breaking into prefectures or town halls, and looting businesses – none of this can be justified.
Following the events of 17 October – which, in some cities, continued late into the night-I wish to express my sincere gratitude and full support to the police officers, gendarmes, and firefighters who intervened under extreme conditions all across France.
By midday – and as early as the morning in Marseille – thousands of far-left individuals, intent on attacking public buildings and confronting our law enforcement, began committing acts of violence.
They were subsequently joined by criminals who looted and ransacked numerous businesses in several French cities, including Paris, Marseille, Lyon, Bordeaux, Rennes, Strasbourg, Grenoble, Nice, Limoges, and many others.
As of now, 1,800 people have been arrested, and investigations are already under way to identify the perpetrators so that they may be held accountable before the justice system.
At this stage, more than 500 police officers, gendarmes, and firefighters have been injured amid this violence.
Sadly, this casualty count is only provisional. The material damage is substantial, affecting, among others, hundreds of business owners.
The Republic will not yield to those who seek to impose disorder and violence.
It’s important to note that protests have also been taking place across Europe .
In Italy rioters clashed with police, looted stores and set property on fire in central Milan on Saturday.
The demonstration escalated after a march against wars and rising living costs began peacefully.
However masked protesters threw stones, paving blocks and other objects at riot police and set fire to barricades made from bar tables. Images of the aftermath showed a severely damaged carabinieri car.
Police used water cannons and teargas to disperse the crowds.
At least two police officers were injured and about 50 demonstrators, including many minors, were detained, the LaPresse news agency reported.
Meanwhile more peaceful protests took place in Portugal , with activists making calls for action to stop rising housing and living costs.
Hundreds of people gathered at Rossio Square in its capital, Lisbon, after a march that had seen thousands take to the streets across the country.
Reports from Agence France-Presse said the group in Lisbon vowed to stay overnight as they gathered around a statue of King Pedro IV in the square.
“The Portuguese social class that pays taxes, that which keeps this country going, is under attack and is losing its rights, notably its right to housing,” said Elena Costa, a 46-year-old social assistant.

The prefect on Sunday said the blaze in the 143-year-old building had been contained.

More than 1,200 people were arrested in France on Saturday after protesters supporting high school students clashed with police, with some demonstrations later spiralling out of control as buildings were set ablaze and shops looted.
Police fired teargas in confrontations with protesters, as demonstrations across France were boosted by other groups angry about high prices and the fraying of a social welfare system. While hundreds of thousands protested peacefully in street marches in scores of cities, violent fringe groups targeted public buildings, luxury boutiques and supermarkets and attacked police vehicles and officers.
Late on Saturday, prime minister Sébastien Lecornu said 1,200 people had been arrested and 150 police hurt.
Interior minister Laurent Nuñez said the official demonstration had been hijacked by casseurs – “ opportunistic delinquents who had seen a chance to pillage and loot … we will find them and deal with them firmly”.
Buildings set ablaze and more than 1,200 arrested as police clash with protesters across France
Police in Paris arrested a “record figure” of 855 people during the protests on Saturday.
Agence France-Presse reported the number detained was the highest ever for a single event.
The figure forms part of the 1,200 arrested across France, as prime minister Sébastien Lecornu said 150 police had been hurt in clashes.
Meanwhile Deputy Mayor of Paris Lamia El Aaraje said the capital had been hit by “a level of violence that I believe we had never seen before”.
France is recovering after its worst protests in years saw buildings attacked and set ablaze across the country.
More than 1,200 people were arrested in the demonstrations on Saturday, which began with protests from students over the cost of living.
However violent fringe groups came out in support of the students, which saw events spiralling out of control.
Whole streets in Paris “have been devastated”, the city’s mayor, Emmanuel Gregoire, said.
Meanwhile in Limoges, central France, the town hall was “largely lost” to a fire set by masked protesters, the top regional official told the AFP news agency.
Authorities in France are now waiting to see if protests will go into another day. The protests began last month at schools ⁠in the poor northern suburbs of Paris , where ⁠anger over teacher ​absences and shabby facilities quickly morphed into a nationwide movement against inequality, weak public spending and falling standards.
We will be following events in France and bringing you any reaction as it comes in.

FOMC Polymarket odds increasingly favor the Federal Reserve leaving interest rates unchanged at its October meeting, with the probability of another rate hike falling sharply despite persistent inflation concerns.
According to the latest Polymarket figures, the odds of the Fed holding rates steady stand at 87%, while the probability of a 25-basis-point increase has dropped to 14%. The market assigns less than a 1% chance to a rate cut or a larger increase.
SOURCE: FOMC Polymarket Odds The figures suggest traders expect Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh and the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) to take a wait-and-see approach at their October 27–28 meeting. The contract has attracted tens of millions of dollars in trading volume, reflecting significant interest in the central bank's next move.
However, expectations have shifted considerably in recent weeks. After hotter-than-expected inflation data, the probability of an October hike climbed toward 50% before retreating as investors reassessed the likelihood of consecutive hikes.
FOMC Polymarket Odds: Inflation Keeps Rate Hike Debate Alive
https://twitterx.com/kucoincom/status/2111064744689795532
The latest US consumer price index (CPI) report showed annual inflation accelerating to 3.7% in September, up from 3.4% in August. Core inflation also increased, reinforcing concerns that price pressures could remain above the Fed's 2% target.
Nevertheless, some policymakers have argued against rushing into another increase. San Francisco Fed President Mary Daly said on October 14 that further hikes could be necessary to control persistent inflation but stressed there was no urgency to act at the upcoming meeting.
That distinction appears central to current market pricing: traders are not ruling out additional tightening, but increasingly expect policymakers to wait for more evidence before moving again.
Got a Gut Feeling? It Could Pay Out Big on Polymarket
Social Media and Market Commentary Reflect Uncertainty
Discussion among prediction-market traders has highlighted the competing arguments. In a recent Reddit discussion in the r/Polymarket community, participants pointed to the September inflation figures and elevated energy costs as reasons a hike could remain possible, while also noting that earlier comments from Fed officials had reduced expectations of immediate action.
Warsh has added another layer of uncertainty by declining to signal the committee's next move publicly. Speaking at an International Monetary Fund event in Bangkok on October 16, he said he does not prejudge individual meetings.
The lack of explicit forward guidance leaves traders particularly sensitive to incoming economic data and any remaining policy signals.
Watch what happens after the announcement pic.twitter.com/uSgRShCqWL
With the October meeting approaching, Polymarket's current pricing makes a pause the clear favorite, though odds can shift quickly as new information emerges.
A fresh inflation surprise could revive bets on a hike, while softer economic data or further calls for patience from policymakers could reinforce expectations of unchanged rates.
For now, traders appear to favor caution over immediate tightening. The key question is whether the Fed sees inflation as sufficiently persistent to justify another hike, or whether policymakers will wait until December before deciding their next move.

items.summary: China is ramping up its presence around Taiwan, in a pattern that Taipei said is designed to 'alter the status quo'.
items.content:
Share ‘Hybrid warfare’: Taiwan drives away 16 Chinese ships on social media
Taiwan's coastguard said it took 'forceful action' to confront Chinese vessels [File: Cheng-chia Huang/AFP]
Taiwan has confronted and driven away 16 Chinese coastguard, research and fishing vessels that it said were involved in simultaneous “maritime harassment” operations.
An “unusually large” number of Chinese vessels took part in coordinated operations around Taiwan’s main island and Pratas (also known as Dongsha), a disputed island to the southwest, the Taiwanese coastguard said in a statement on Sunday.

The Chinese vessels included four fishing boats, which engaged in “simultaneous operations’ that the coastguard described as “hybrid warfare”.
Taiwan’s coastguard said its vessels took “forceful action immediately to effectively neutralise the threats” and accused Beijing of “attempting to unilaterally alter the status quo” in the Taiwan Strait and give the “false impression of jurisdiction”.
Some of the vessels reportedly entered Taiwan’s restricted waters.
Beijing claims Taiwan and Pratas as part of its territory and asserts jurisdiction over the surrounding waters, which Taipei rejects. China has long threatened to use force to regain control of Taiwan.
In an incident on October 1 , Taiwan’s coastguard fired water cannon at a Chinese recreational fishing vessel near Pratas island between Taiwan and mainland China that Beijing claims.
China has intensified its maritime pressure on Taiwan in recent months. Beijing deployed a record 244 coastguard, scientific research and other ships around Taiwan’s main island in July, Taiwanese official data show, compared with just 58 in the same month last year.
In the first 21 days of August, 152 vessels were detected; most were from the Chinese Coastguard, but fishing boats and research vessels were also involved.
China also deploys warships around Taiwan on a near-daily basis, but those are counted separately.

Shabana Mahmood to hold talks with EU over law enforcement cooperation
UK home secretary’s meeting comes after PM said he wanted to rejoin European law enforcement databases
The UK home secretary, Shabana Mahmood , will meet the EU’s home affairs commissioner on Monday for further talks just days after Andy Burnham said he wanted to rejoin European law enforcement databases from which the UK has been locked out of since Brexit.
According to the European Commission , they will discuss “migration, border management, law enforcement cooperation and counter-terrorism”, with the latest Frontex data published on Monday showing a 43% decline in small boats crossing the Channel.
It will be the second time Mahmood has met Magnus Brunner in two months and comes amid an increase in engagement between London and Brussels since Andy Burnham announced he would use an upcoming EU-UK summit to “ lay out to the country ” what he believes are the “different options for Britain’s long-term relationship” with the EU.
Brexit’s back – but are British voters ready to contemplate a reversal?
Brunner said “the UK’s contribution is indispensable” to continuing efforts to suppress irregular migration after the EU introduced a suite of new laws aimed at speeding up asylum decisions and deportations.
On the agenda for Monday’s meeting will be talks on the UK rejoining some of the police and security databases it was locked out from after Brexit and rejoining a new database, Eurodac , centring on migration.
Last week Burnham told MPs that “one of the most positive aspects of my meeting with [the European Commission] president [Ursula] von der Leyen in New York, was her openness to the conversation about restoring data sharing on immigration across the UK, across Europe”.
He said it was “control” that the UK “lost” and should get “more attention” in the debate about Brexit . “I will work hard to see if we can get a practical arrangement on that very issue at the summit in November,” Burnham said.
Magnus Brunner will discuss ‘migration, border management, law enforcement cooperation and counter-terrorism’ with Shabana Mahmood, according to the European Commission. Photograph: Dursun Aydemir/Anadolu/Getty Images Brunner will also meet the MI5 director general, Ken McCallum, and visit the National Counter Terrorism Security Office, as well as meet senior officials from the UK’s child sexual abuse centre to discuss joint efforts to tackle such crimes.
He has also been chosen to deliver a lecture at King’s College London on migration and asylum, where he will talk about the impact of the EU’s new Pact on Migration and Asylum, a framework of 10 pieces of legislation overhauling how the EU manages its borders, processes asylum applications and shares information among member states.
Brunner will tell those he meets that the new laws have already had a significant impact along with a shift in political priorities around migration in key countries such as Germany, Italy and France.
He said the “reforms are paying” off in the UK too, with illegal crossings down 43%.
“We must stay on this course, including along all relevant migration routes, and the UK’s contribution is indispensable,” he said. “We have put our European house in order. Illegal crossings at our external borders are down 55% over two years, with a further third this year, and asylum applications are at record lows in the countries that used to be main destinations.”
One key database the UK wants access to is Eurodac, a new platform which collects fingerprints and facial images of asylum seekers from the age of six, and security flags for people linked to terrorism or serious crime.
Another is the Schengen Information System (SIS), which contains data on missing persons, stolen goods, vehicles and number plates, and fugitives crossing internal EU borders. About 20m searches are made daily on the SIS, according to EU data, mostly on cars.

Vance acknowledges ‘failures’ in US handling of Iran war
US vice president admits positioning of US troops exposed weaknesses in military’s approach
ISTANBUL US Vice President JD Vance acknowledged “a lot of mistakes and a lot of fundamental failures” in the handling of the Iran war, as he faced questions over the conflict’s rising human and economic costs during a CBS News town hall.
Vance made the remarks in response to Joey Amor, whose wife, Master Sgt. Nicole Amor, was among six US Army Reserve soldiers killed in an Iranian strike on a military site in Kuwait in the opening hours of the war that began in late February. At least 21 US service members have been killed and hundreds wounded so far.
Amor questioned reports that the facility had not been adequately secured, demanding accountability from the Trump administration.
“Though the Iranian drone was the weapon that killed my wife, there were a lot of mistakes and a lot of fundamental failures that led up to that,” Amor said.
Vance acknowledged that there were shortcomings. “Sometimes information doesn't filter up to me,” he said, pledging to “take every single failure extremely seriously.”
The vice president also admitted that the positioning of US troops exposed weaknesses in the military’s approach. “I know that there are some issues with, for example … where troops were located that we realized was a huge mistake and that we could do better on. And we have changed that,” he said.
Vance pointed to the growing threat posed by inexpensive drones, saying the US military had altered its tactics to better protect troops and prevent further casualties.
Asked why Washington had still not secured a decisive victory despite President Donald Trump’s initial expectations, Vance argued that the US had “in some ways … won decisively,” but acknowledged the outcome also depended on Iran’s actions. “The enemy gets a vote here,” he said.
Vance defended the administration’s strategy, saying Washington was seeking a “final firm commitment from the Iranians that they're not going to rebuild their nuclear program.”

items.summary: Retirees Return to the Streets in Iran as Regime Warns of Falling Trust and Presses Nightly Mobilization  <font c
items.content:
Home Iran News Now Iran Economy News Retirees Return to the Streets in Iran as Regime Warns of Falling...
Retirees Return to the Streets in Iran as Regime Warns of Falling Trust and Presses Nightly Mobilization
Steel factory retirees and employees in Isfahan held a protest rally on September 16, 2026
Retirees protested across Isfahan, Shush, Kermanshah, Tehran, Rasht and Ahvaz on October 18, alongside other labor and consumer protests, as economic grievances continued to spill into explicitly political slogans. In Isfahan, steel and mining retirees chanted “The enemy is right here; they lie and say it’s America” and “Only in the street will we get our rights.” In Shush, Social Security retirees demanded “welfare with dignity,” while other gatherings targeted corruption, inflation and collapsing purchasing power. The protests are cutting across pension, labor and livelihood issues while increasingly rejecting the regime’s effort to attribute domestic hardship primarily to foreign pressure.
That sensitivity is visible at the top. The Assembly of Experts issued a statement acknowledging that inflation, purchasing-power losses, housing, employment and production problems are eroding public trust, while also warning that national problems must not become victims of “factional disputes” and “erosive rivalries.” More revealingly, it called for the regime’s nightly street mobilizations to continue “until threats are removed” and “full security is established,” describing them as a source of support for the armed forces and officials. The language shows that these gatherings are being treated as part of the regime’s domestic security architecture.
That effort at staged unity is itself being undermined by factional attacks. Pro-regime gatherings have featured slogans branding Mohammad-Javad Zarif a “traitor” and accusing him of serving America, even as senior institutions as well as the regime's supreme leader demand cohesion.
Iran’s regime is acting like one afraid of the next eruption: 11 people arrested months after #IranProtests and branded part of a foreign “coup,” 44 million screened for extra food aid, and hardliners accusing rival insiders of serving Washington. The fear is that these pressures…
The deterioration is also visible in Tehran’s school system. Governor Mohammad-Sadegh Motamedian said the capital has 7,000 fewer students this academic year while the surrounding counties gained 17,000, attributing part of the shift to economic pressure pushing families out of Tehran. He said the province still needs about 9,000 classrooms and 638 schools, while 80 schools promised by Tehran municipality have not been delivered. This is not just an education statistic; it is evidence of households being displaced by living costs while public infrastructure fails to keep pace with the migration.
The nursing crisis is deeper than the 700-person shortage reported in Bushehr. The head of Bushehr University of Medical Sciences told IRNA that the province cannot attract enough nurses because pay is too low compared with nearby oil and petrochemical jobs. Nationally, Nursing House secretary-general Mohammad Sharifi-Moghaddam has said roughly 70,000 nurses are outside the profession, with average monthly pay around 25–28 million tomans and resignation rates continuing to rise. The significance is institutional: a health system already struggling with shortages is losing trained staff because the profession no longer provides a sustainable livelihood.
Food consumption tells a similar story. The Health Ministry says Iranians consume only about one serving of dairy per day, well below recommended levels. Price pressures are a major constraint: official data shows dairy prices up 147% year-on-year, while food inflation reached 134% nationally and 140% in rural areas. The production base has also contracted sharply. Dairy industry spokesman Mohammadreza Bani-Tabaa says nearly 80% of dairy companies have closed over the past two decades, reducing the number from around 1,000 to roughly 200. Consumption is falling at the same time productive capacity has been hollowed out.
Pezeshkian lists Iran’s fault lines—power, water, gas, fuel, banking, budget, pensions—as a cleric is stabbed to death in Sari. Central Bank’s goal: just slow the #inflation rate. By @MansoreGolestan https://t.co/eBARBew5k6
Iran’s oil position is becoming more precarious. The latest tanker-tracking data reported by Reuters indicate that crude exports have effectively fallen to zero under the US naval blockade, while only limited LPG and jet-fuel cargoes have managed to get through. At least eight LPG tankers and one jet-fuel tanker reportedly breached the blockade, but the volumes are far too small to replace crude revenues.
The regime has already acknowledged the underlying problem. Central Bank governor Abdolnaser Hemmati said earlier that oil income had fallen to zero and that crude exports had “practically stopped,” even as Tasnim continued to highlight earlier budget oil receipts. Separate data show crude production falling below 2 million barrels per day, compared with roughly 3.26 million a year earlier. The political significance is straightforward: oil revenues fund salaries, pensions, subsidies, imports and the security state. A prolonged cutoff narrows the regime’s room to buy social peace precisely when protests and welfare demands are rising.
Tehran’s response to the rial’s slide past 270,000 tomans isn’t restoring confidence—it’s rationing it. A $2B dollar sale that fades in days. A $10k purchase scheme that requires 2.5 billion tomans most people don’t have. A crackdown on #Tether and gold. All while chasing $21B in…
Parliament meanwhile approved Mehrdad Akhlaghi as defense minister by 237 votes to 15, replacing Aziz Nasirzadeh, who was killed during the war. Akhlaghi immediately issued threats toward US forces, while Mohsen Rezaei claimed Iran had prepared a military plan more destructive than previous rounds of fighting.
The broader picture is of a regime reeling under mounting socio-economic pressure and deepening internal conflict, yet responding by keeping both warmongering and repression at full intensity. Rather than easing tensions or addressing the structural causes of discontent, the leadership continues to threaten external escalation while tightening control at home. The logic appears defensive: in a system already worried about unrest, factional fracture and declining authority, any visible retreat risks being read as weakness.

items.summary: <a href="https://news.google.
items.content:
Share What help can Egypt offer Saudi Arabia in the war against the Houthis? on social media
Egyptian President Abdel Fattah wl-Sisi meets Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman in Cairo, Egypt on September 15, 2026 [Bandar Algaloud/Saudi Royal Court/Reuters]
Egypt’s parliament is convening on Sunday after President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi requested an emergency session to approve defensive military aid to Saudi Arabia, if Riyadh asks for support in its war with Yemen’s Houthis.
The request comes as the Iran-backed armed group continues attacks on Saudi Arabia, including the capital, Riyadh, and its airports and oil facilities.
list of 3 items list 1 of 3 How far will Egypt go to help Saudi Arabia secure the Red Sea?
list 2 of 3 Egypt’s el-Sisi vows to defend Saudi Arabia from Houthi attacks
list 3 of 3 Saudi-led coalition intercepts drones as Egypt weighs sending help
El-Sisi declared that Egypt will “carry out any measure to protect” Saudi Arabia, in a speech on Saturday, but said that he “hopes” the parliament will give him authorisation to proceed.
On Sunday, Egypt said it would provide “all necessary and possible support to Saudi Arabia to defend its safety and stability”. The National Defence Council, chaired by President el-Sisi, said it “stands fully with” Saudi Arabia to defend its resources, territorial integrity and Islamic holy sites.
But what would Egyptian assistance look like? And what capacity does it have to “protect” Saudi Arabia in its war with the Houthis?
What’s behind el-Sisi’s decision to offer help to Saudi Arabia?
Saudi Arabia has long been a strategic and economic partner of Egypt, and el-Sisi said in a statement last month that Saudi security is “integral” to Egypt’s security.
Political analyst and Gulf studies expert Thomas Bonnie James told Al Jazeera that the Houthi security threat to the kingdom is one of the “converging” pressures that have led to this decision. The other one, is economics.
“Houthi pressure on [Bab] al-Mandeb threatens the Suez Canal , which Egypt’s foreign minister says has lost about $11bn since the attacks began in 2023,” he said, referring to Houthi attacks on Israeli-linked ships passing through the narrow strait, carried out in solidarity with Gaza.
James suggested that the decision is also important to Cairo, because “millions of Egyptians live and work in Saudi Arabia, which is Egypt’s largest single source of remittances. An Egyptian resident was killed, and others were injured in the attacks on Riyadh’s airport.”
He also said that Egypt does not want to be seen as the regional ally that “stood aside while others defended the kingdom,” as Turkiye and Pakistan have made their own pledges after activating the Mecca defence pact signed in August amid the deteriorating security situation in the Middle East.
Hostilities in Yemen continue to escalate. Two air raids by the Saudi-led coalition hit Hodeidah in the southwest on Sunday.
Saudi forces also intercepted drones near Riyadh and Eastern provinces. The capital’s King Khalid international airport has come under attack at least 20 times since fighting flared between the internationally recognised government and the Houthis, also known as Ansar Allah – Arabic for Supporters of God.
The Saudi-backed forces are fighting the Houthis on several fronts, including Taiz and Marib, and some analysts argue the Houthis are stretched thin after their summer gains.
But James told Al Jazeera “that defeating them outright is a tall order”.
“Ground forces backed by air power can retake the coastline; stopping missiles launched from the mountains is much harder,” he said.
They will be convening on Sunday at 1pm local time (10am GMT).
Under the Egyptian law, the President cannot declare war or send the military on foreign missions without the approval from the parliament.
For the authorisation to be granted, at least two-thirds of the politicians in the House of Representatives must vote in favour of the proposal.
Does Egypt have security cooperation with Saudi Arabia?
Not exactly. Egypt and Saudi Arabia have not signed a formal bilateral or multilateral pact on defence cooperation. But Cairo has a long history of cooperation with Riyadh.
Egypt is a founding member of the Multinational Maritime Defense Coalition, which Saudi Arabia launched in July. It aims to protect shipping in the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandeb – territories on Yemen’s coastline. Houthis captured towns and cities near Bab al-Mandeb last month, but the internationally recognised government has since wrested control of some of the areas from the Iran-backed group.
Egypt also participated in joint military exercises with Saudi Arabia in 2024.
Cairo was also part of a 2015 coalition , cobled together after the Houthi group captured large areas of north and western Yemen, including the capital Sanaa in September 2024. Egypt contributed naval and air forces to help secure maritime corridors in the Red Sea against the Houthis.
But James, the Gulf studies expert, told Al Jazeera that what el-Sisi is proposing is different from the maritime defence coalition Egypt recently joined.
“He is hoping for authorisation to deploy Egyptian forces to help defend Saudi territory itself,” he said. “It would move Egypt from a multilateral maritime framework to a bilateral military commitment.”
What will be the nature of Egyptian assistance to Saudi Arabia?
El-Sisi explicitly said that he is only proposing “defence” and that he isn’t “speaking in order for us to fight anyone or attack anyone”.
Military Defence Analyst Alexandru Hudisteanu said that the use of counter-drones and anti-missile support is a high probability if the decision is authorised.
“It would be the most urgent need at this point to make sure that the defence of Saudi Arabia is backed up and reinforced,” he told Al Jazeera.
Simultaneously, he added that the request itself is also a strategic move of deterrence.
“We know Saudi Arabia has one of the most prolific militaries out there in terms of capacities and capabilities. It’s a matter of the territory which Saudi Arabia needs to cover at any given moment,” Hudisteanu said.
James said that any contribution by Egypt would focus on the protection of Saudi territory, using “air and missile defence around critical infrastructure, intercepting drones, naval escort and intelligence sharing”.
James said that it is unlikely Egypt will deploy troops to Yemen’s front lines.
In the 1960s, former Egyptian President Gamal Abdel Nasser deployed tens of thousands of troops in the Yemen Civil War. Saudi Arabia backed the rival side. Egypt suffered heavy casualties and Saudi-Egyptian ties were strained.
“What Egypt will not want is to send troops into Yemen. Nasser’s intervention there in the 1960s sends a clear message: defend the kingdom, don’t take ownership of Yemen,” he told Al Jazeera.

Michael Burry Warns of a Stock Market ‘Supervolcano’
Photo by BeInCrypto Michael Burry, who bet against the 2008 housing bubble, says the next bear market may last a long time. The Michael Burry bear market warning rests on a century of inflation-adjusted S&P 500 data.
On the surface, stocks look calm. The S&P 500 closed at a record on October 6. Yet Burry argues that fewer stocks now carry the index higher.
Burry compares the market to a supervolcano caldera. The ground looks peaceful, while pressure builds underneath.
He says the same hidden buildup sat beneath each of the 10 market tops of the past 40 years.
In his latest Substack post, he calls the October 6 high unremarkable. Volume stayed light, and similar highs in June and August 2026 led only to brief pauses.
However, his chart tracks market breadth, meaning how many stocks join a rally. That breadth keeps shrinking, echoing a similar market breadth argument from gold advocate Peter Schiff.
The Michael Burry bear market case also cites speculation, stretched valuations, and returning inflation. Earlier this month, he said investors had entered a denial stage resembling 2000 and 2008.
Michael Burry Bear Market History Points to a Long Wait
Burry leans on history, a field he says chart-trading algorithms largely ignore.
From 1966 to 1982, the inflation-adjusted S&P 500 fell about 53%. Between 1929 and 1949, the real price return reached negative 58%.
More recently, real prices dropped roughly 40% from the 2000 peak to the 2011 trough.
Dividends soften those losses. With reinvestment, the 1966 to 1982 decline shrinks to about 10%. Similarly, the 2000 to 2011 loss falls to about 25%.
Real S&P 500 Bear Markets. Source: BeInCrypto Still, the Michael Burry bear market thesis centers on time, not wipeouts. Each episode forced patient holders into a wait lasting many years.
That lesson clashes with today's "buy the dip" culture. Meanwhile, Panmure Liberum recently made Wall Street's most bearish call, a 5,000-point S&P 500 target for 2027.
If 15 to 20 years of weak real returns lie ahead, Burry argues investors should know now. For crypto holders, the open question is whether digital assets would decouple.
Bitwise CIO Matt Hougan, for one, argued that Bitcoin thrives across economic scenarios. A Michael Burry bear market lasting a decade would put that claim to its hardest test.

The U.S. Treasury Secretary warned Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to "be very careful" in public statements about U.S. support for Ukraine.
SpaceX's military-tier internet service, provided by the U.S., was recently restricted in Ukraine,  hindering the country’s ability to use drones in defense against Russian assaults.

U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent warned Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Sunday to "be careful" in public statements about U.S. support for Ukraine .
U.S.-provided Starlink internet was recently restricted in Ukraine, hindering the war-torn country's ability to respond to Russian assaults. Ukraine uses Starshield, the military and government-controlled version of the commercial Starlink, to conduct military operations.
In an earlier interview on NBC's "Meet the Press," Zelenskyy said he believed the U.S. government was responsible for the slowdown, and that Ukraine was "blocked" from U.S. intelligence for a period of time. Zelenskyy said Starshield-linked vehicles and drones are still being restricted in speed.

Bessent cautioned Zelenskyy about making those claims.
"President [Donald] Trump and Secretary [Marco] Rubio have categorically said that no one under the Trump administration did that, and I think it is very reckless for President Zelenskyy to make such a charge," Bessent said on "Meet the Press."
"President Zelenskyy should be very careful about making statements like this that aren't true," he added.
Starlink, high-speed satellite internet provided by Elon Musk's SpaceX , is critical to Ukraine's defense. Musk himself said in a post on X last week that the U.S. government and President Donald Trump are "ultimately" responsible for any slowdowns to the military version of Starlink known as Starshield .
"Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government," Musk wrote. "Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS."
SpaceX did not respond to a request for comment from CNBC.
Reuters reported last week that the White House ordered the technology restrictions, but Trump has denied responsibility for the slowdown.
"Well, I don't know if it was anybody because it wasn't me, and I don't think it was Elon," the president said last week. "And from what I understand, it's the same as it's always been."
The U.S. relationship with Ukraine has been highly scrutinized throughout Trump's second term, as he has frequently antagonized the war-torn country while pushing for a peace deal.
Trump has recently expressed frustration over Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries as he faces pressure from voters over sky-high gasoline and diesel prices ahead of the U.S. midterm elections. The president has even personally blamed Zelenskyy for the rise in energy prices: "He wants to make problems for the world. He wants to make problems for our farmers, our ranchers, with diesel fuel," Trump said.
Soaring energy prices are largely due to the U.S. war with Iran, which severely disrupted the Strait of Hormuz and choked oil shipments from the Persian Gulf. The national average for a gallon of gas in the U.S. was nearly $4.30 on Sunday, according to AAA . Diesel was roughly $6.32 per gallon, about 20 cents off September's record high.
Trump has tried to offset the energy pinch by importing Russian diesel. In a post on Truth Social earlier in the month, he said: "Diesel Prices for Americans and, indeed, the World, will be COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST!"

"Beyond irresponsible. What part of enforcing a law passed 86-11 by the Senate does the President and his advisors not understand?" Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., said in a post on X .
