items.title: Better AI Chip Stock: Taiwan Semiconductor vs. Micron - The Motley Fool
items.summary: Better AI Chip Stock: Taiwan Semiconductor vs. Micron  The Motley Fool
items.content:
While companies like Nvidia and  AMD may get most of the headline glory in the AI realm for their powerful processors, the reality is these companies only design some of the chips that go into data centers. The fabrication muscle in the sector lies in a handful of chip foundry businesses, with Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing ( TSM -2.28% ) and Micron ( MU -5.63% ) being the two largest in the world by market cap.
But which one makes for the better buy? Let's dig in, as these two are very different investments.
Micron and Taiwan Semiconductor aren't competitors
On the surface, Micron and Taiwan Semiconductor are both chip foundry companies. Both take in client orders, then create their chips. However, that's where the similarities end.
Micron and Taiwan Semiconductor produce two entirely different types of chips; Micron designs and makes memory chips, and Taiwan Semiconductor makes logic chips designed by other companies. Both are required in accelerated computing units like GPUs, but each serves a different role.
Furthermore, the technologies behind each one are radically different. There isn't a ton that separates one memory chip from another. Take basic computer RAM, for example. Nobody cares a lot about which brand of RAM is in a laptop, only what capacity that RAM has. That's because most memory chips are practically the same, although Micron is challenging that notion. It recently agreed to design an industry-first custom memory chip for Nvidia's GPUs, which could be a different avenue to lock in better long-term contract deals.
Market cap Market cap calculated using publicly traded shares outstanding only. Does not include unlisted, private, or dual-class non-traded shares. Implied market cap may vary. $994.34B
Because one manufacturer's memory chips are much like another's, they are subject to commodity-like pricing. This year, demand for memory chips has steeply outpaced supply, causing prices to soar. The shortage is expected to get worse in 2027 and 2028, which would allow Micron to keep turning huge profits on its chips.
The logic chips that come out of Taiwan Semiconductor's foundries are completely different. Companies like Nvidia and AMD design processors, and their various devices can deliver competitive edges on a range of criteria as the chipmakers work to improve speed, energy efficiency, transistor density, and more. Choosing a reliable chip manufacturer is a big part of this design process, and with TSMC's massive production facilities, proven track record, and leading technology, it's the partner that is most often selected. However, TSMC has relatively greater production capacity than the memory chip industry, and has been expanding production capacity in recent years, so it was able to mostly handle the AI demand rush.
Market cap Market cap calculated using publicly traded shares outstanding only. Does not include unlisted, private, or dual-class non-traded shares. Implied market cap may vary. $2.14T
Micron holds an edge in the revenue growth department, as it's still benefiting from the effect of soaring memory chip prices due to the shortage. However, TSMC's growth rate isn't bad either.
TSM Revenue (Quarterly YoY Growth) data by YCharts.
Another area where Micron holds an edge is valuation. Investors today can pick up Micron shares at a much cheaper 5.3 times forward earnings compared to TSMC's 24.
Why the huge price discrepancy? It all has to do with Micron operating in what has historically been a highly cyclical industry. Every time memory demand outpaces supply, the chipmakers start to build new fabs. By the time they come online, the demand waves have often slackened, supply leaps ahead, and prices tumble.
The market isn't convinced that the current wave of intense memory chip demand driven by the AI infrastructure build-out will last, and it's discounting it as a result. But Micron and others in the memory industry have said the shortage is going to get worse before it gets better. If Micron's stock rises throughout the year due to strong demand, it could deliver incredible returns.
TSMC is also a solid investment, and because the logic chip industry is not as cyclical (it still is, but not to the same degree), the market is not as concerned about its outlook, and therefore is not valuing the stock at a discount.
I think this is a huge mismatch, and Micron makes for the better buy, at least when upside potential is considered. While TSMC is still a fantastic investment, the mismatch between Micron's stock price and its earnings potential is just too much to ignore. Investors should pounce on the deal.

Greens senator Jordon Steele-John has released a statement addressing a letter that contained complaints about his alleged behaviour towards women. Photograph: Mick Tsikas/AAP
Greens senator Jordon Steele-John has released a statement addressing a letter that contained complaints about his alleged behaviour towards women. Photograph: Mick Tsikas/AAP
Jordon Steele-John says ‘I’m not on leave’ and accuses Greens leader of making ‘bad call’ regarding complaints
Greens senator for WA says complaints regarding his behaviour towards women not about ‘accountability’ but rather ‘factionalism’
Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast
Jordon Steele-John has accused an internal faction within the Greens of playing “nasty political games” and the leader, David Shoebridge, of pressuring him to take leave after complaints about his conduct were made public last week.
The 32-year-old Greens senator released a six-page statement on Sunday night after Nine newspapers reported last week that seven former and current party members had demanded an investigation into allegations he had acted inappropriately towards women between 2017 and 2025.
The complaints are now subject to an independent investigation commissioned by the Western Australian Greens and have been referred to the Independent Parliamentary Standards Commission .
Steele-John said in the statement he wanted any alleged behaviour investigated “fairly and thoroughly” but claimed an “unofficial faction” within the WA branch had released the complaint letter to the media in a bid to oust him from the Senate.
Greens senator Jordon Steele-John takes leave amid investigation into complaints
“It is no coincidence that the letter arrived at the leader’s office the day after we agreed on the timeline for the next preselection,” Steele-John said on Sunday.
“It is my opinion that this is an attempt to influence forthcoming party preselections by deliberately leaking out of context or misleading information to smear potential candidates and myself.”
Steele-John said some of the letter’s authors and signatories may have signed the letter out of “genuine commitment” to people who experienced violence but he was angry it had been politicised.
“When processes meant to protect victims are turned into weapons in preselection contests, everyone loses. Survivors become less likely to be believed. Real complaints are treated with suspicion. And the people who did this know it,” he said.
“That is not accountability. It is factionalism, and it has no place in the Greens.”
The senator said he was not on leave, contrary to Shoebridge’s comments last week, and that he had been pressured by the leader to request leave on Thursday as Nine’s story was breaking.
“I feel that he used those meetings to repeatedly pressure me to say that I would take leave,” Steele-John said.
The senator said “survivors of family violence are entitled to make decisions about their own lives and the Greens have always said so”.
“It was a bad call from David. We’ve all made those in politics. So, to be clear, I am not on leave and did not agree to the inclusion of that line within David’s statement.”
Shoebridge said on Thursday that Steele-John had requested leave from the party room “and I have accepted it”.
“Senator Steele-John has indicated to me that he’s on leave, and that leave means leave,” the Greens leader said on Friday.
Guardian Australia contacted Shoebridge’s office for comment on Sunday night.
Steele-John said the letter of complaint to Shoebridge referred to three matters but it did not set out any allegations in detail.
Addressing a disparaging nickname – “feels on wheels” – the senator said he believed it originated because he was emotional during speeches early in his career regarding the disability royal commission. The nickname, however, had taken on a new meaning in recent time, he said in Sunday’s statement.
“Over the years, this nickname would periodically resurface like strategic clockwork, growing in lore each time.
“Eventually, I was informed that this phrase, which mocked my disability and my emotions, had taken on a new, more sinister meaning: that I had treated women inappropriately.”
Steele-John said another matter contained in the letter related to alleged sexual harassment at a Greens campaign party in 2024; however, the authors did not outline specific allegations.
The senator said the final matter related to alleged “serious sexual misconduct”.
An investigation into alleged sexual assault was ultimately closed by the Western Australian police with a finding of no charges, he said. Comment was sought from WA police.
“It took people close to me to make me realise that I was experiencing domestic violence,” Steele-John said in Sunday’s statement.
Nine last week reported on the existence of a 47-page “secret dossier”, first drafted in 2016 , which the newspaper said contained allegations against Steele-John and how the party should respond if they were to come to light.
Steele-John said on Sunday he had an “interpersonal conflict” between himself and two friends in 2016 before he was preselected. The senator alleged the unofficial faction had attempted to shop the “half-heard rumours” of the conflict to journalists in 2017 as part of a “smear campaign”.
As a result, Steele-John said, the document was created so the party office and staff had “the same accurate information to give anyone who had heard the rumours and was concerned”.

The national average for a gallon of gas in the U.S. was nearly $4.30 on Sunday, according to AAA . Diesel was roughly $6.32 per gallon, about 20 cents off September's record high.
Trump has tried to offset the energy pinch by importing Russian diesel. In a post on Truth Social earlier in the month, he said: "Diesel Prices for Americans and, indeed, the World, will be COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST!"
Many U.S. lawmakers, including Republicans, have condemned the president's plan to buy Russian diesel. Congress recently sent Trump an overwhelmingly bipartisan sanctions package aimed at crippling Russia's energy industry. Trump signed the bill into law, but waived portions of it over the weekend, citing the national interest in an explanation to Congress.
"Beyond irresponsible. What part of enforcing a law passed 86-11 by the Senate does the President and his advisors not understand?" Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., said in a post on X . "It's unconscionable that this administration is capitulating to a Russian dictator who illegally invaded Ukraine and butchers innocent civilians every single day."

items.title: Oil facilities hit in deadly overnight attack on St Petersburg
items.summary: At least one person was killed in the strikes, which also hit a data centre used by Russia's equivalent of Facebook.
items.content:
Image caption, The St Petersburg Oil Terminal was among targets hit in the city overnight
At least one person has been killed in an overnight attack on St Petersburg that successfully targeted two of the city's oil facilities.
The region's Governor Alexander Beglov said fires were being extinguished at the St Petersburg Oil Terminal and the Ruchyi oil depot following the attack, which also injured at least five.
A logistics centre belonging to Ozon - known as Russia's Amazon - and a data centre belonging to Facebook equivalent VKontakte were also hit.
Kyiv has not yet commented on the strikes. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Saturday morning that Russia had targeted his country's energy sector 76 times since Donald Trump declared an "energy ceasefire" last week.
Ukraine had paused its strikes on Russian oil facilities - which it says are to limit the main revenue stream for Moscow's war effort - for three days after the announcement, while accusing Russia of continuing.
It then resumed strikes earlier this week, drawing the ire of Trump, who called for a truce to facilitate a deal he struck with his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin to supply diesel.
Ukraine has struck St Petersburg before, though regions closer to Ukraine are threatened more often. The city's oil terminal was last hit in July .
Russia's defence ministry said it had shot down more than 1,000 Ukrainian drones over Russian territory overnight into Sunday.
St Petersburg's governor said 12 apartment buildings and two homes were damaged in the attacks on the city, while Pulkovo Airport was temporarily closed.
He also said mobile internet service disruption was possible.
Social network VK confirmed a drone had targeted its regional data centre, but stressed its services were available "as usual" after users reported outages in the early hours of the morning.
Ozon also confirmed its local logistics centre had been targeted by a drone, sparking a fire.
It said staff were evacuated and no one was injured, and that it was not accepting shipments from sellers at the location "as it is currently serving other operational purposes".
As well as numerous oil facilities across Russia, Ukraine has also mounted strikes aimed at disrupting the Russian economy more broadly. Earlier this month, it launched a series of attacks on Yandex, Russia's largest search engine, that led to service disruptions.
Relations between Washington and Kyiv have frayed since the US struck a controversial deal to import Russian diesel in the hope of bringing down US energy prices, which have skyrocketed during the Iran war, ahead of the midterm elections.
Zelensky suggested the deal was tantamount to the US investing in Russia's war effort.
Trump's decision to temporarily suspend a raft of sanctions against Russia has brought fresh criticism , including from some US Republicans.
However, on Sunday, Zelensky said on Telegram he had had conversations with Trump's top negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner.
He said their teams are in constant communication and preparing the next diplomatic steps.
Both Russia and Ukraine have been striking one another's energy infrastructure with increasing intensity ahead of the winter, as Moscow's full-scale invasion drags on in its fifth year.
Russia says it hits targets used by Ukraine's military, though the UN noted on Friday that the first two weeks of October had been the deadliest for Ukrainian civilians in years.
Russian strikes on energy facilities have left hundreds of thousands without power, raising concerns about civilians enduring another freezing winter.
Zelensky said on Saturday that tens of thousands of people were still without power. Russia launched nearly 2,700 drones, 1,700 aerial bombs and 66 missiles in the past week, most of which were aimed at energy facilities, he said.

A gleaning group has saved Â£1m worth of fruit and vegetables that would have been left in field and donated them to food banks.
Gleaning Cornwall relies on volunteers to collect unwanted produce from harvested fields, delivering it to 160 food banks, community larders and kitchens across the South West.
Despite reaching the seven-figure milestone, the group has warned more funding is needed in order to keep up with demand.
Reliance on food banks is increasing and since 2015 the number of known settings providing food aid in Cornwall has risen from 20 to 180, according to Cornwall Council.
Image caption, The gleaning group has saved 460 tonnes of produce since the start of 2020
Gleaning Cornwall started in 2020 and said it had repurposed more than 460 tonnes of produce since then.
But the charity's founder, Holly Whitelaw, warned it was now threatened by economic constraints.
"There is less money around and we need to do more with it," she said. "Our infrastructure urgently needs funding if we are to keep going."
The charity said it fed 11,000 people every week with the stipulation that all its produce must be completely free to recipients.
However, the organisation said the cost of transport, storage and coordination was rising sharply.
It comes at a time when food bank usage is higher than ever with statistics from Cornwall's Trussell Trust showing its food banks distributed more than 35,500 emergency food parcels between April 2024 and March 2025.
A study by Cornwall Council found that 30% of children in the county are living in food poverty.
Whitelaw encouraged people to play their part by reducing the amount of food they wasted at home.
She said: "If we waste food, we waste the substantial energy that went into producing it.
"Utilising what we already have saves money and helps the environment."

items.content:
Netanyahu: Russia aiding Iran's antisemitic bot networks, acting against Israeli interests
The prime minister criticized Russia's ties with Tehran and antisemitic online campaigns targeting Israel, warning that Iran could eventually seek to destabilize Russia itself.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu seen during a presentation of Israel’s national security doctrine, in Jerusalem, October 18, 2026
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said that Israel’s and Russia’s interests have clashed several times recently, and that Moscow has also taken steps against Israel , during a Sunday presentation of Israel’s national security doctrine.
“ Russia’s cooperation with Iran is something that runs counter to its interests, as does the existence of bot networks conducting a campaign against the State of Israel with the most blatant antisemitism imaginable,” Netanyahu said in response to a question from The Jerusalem Post . “We raise all these issues with them, and we do so very clearly,” the prime minister added.
Netanyahu said that he and Russian President Vladimir Putin “speak when necessary.”
“Russia has its own interests, and the State of Israel has its interests, and they do not always overlap. Sometimes they even clash,” Netanyahu said. “That is why I always try to pursue our shared interests to the fullest extent possible. If that is not possible, you stand by your own interests and fight to defend them.”
The prime minister also stressed that Russia understands that there are shared interests that could be jeopardized, for example, if an Islamist Iran were to become a nuclear power.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu seen during a presentation of Israel’s national security doctrine, in Jerusalem, October 18, 2026 (credit: MA'AYAN TOAF/GPO)
“My assessment, and I do not want to speak on behalf of others, is that, given the Muslim population within Russia itself, Iran would also seek to turn elements within that population into its agents.
"This is because Iran holds extreme ideological views concerning the conquest of the world, the subjugation of all Muslims to its doctrine, and the imposition of that doctrine on all nonbelievers,” Netanyahu said.
Russia's growing military cooperation with Iran emerging as significant concern for Israel
Russia’s growing military cooperation with Iran has emerged as a significant concern for Israel, particularly amid reports that Moscow is helping Tehran strengthen its military capabilities , improve its drone and missile technology, and obtain intelligence that could support attacks against American and allied forces in the Middle East.
The Institute for the Study of War (ISW) published a report saying Russia has continued providing Iran with military equipment and components. A report published in August, citing a European government document and a Western official, said that Russian shipments to Iran via the Caspian Sea included drone components, ammunition and explosives.
As of July, more than two dozen Russian vessels reportedly transported cargo to Iran’s Amirabad port.
A Reuters investigation reported in July that US intelligence officials were examining whether Russia had provided Iran with targeting information or technology that improved the accuracy and resistance to jamming of Iranian Shahed drones.
Russian President Vladimir Putin speaks with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian during a meeting in Turkmenbashi, Turkmenistan, October 8, 2026; illustrative. (credit: SPUTNIK/GAVRIIL GRIGOROV/POOL VIA REUTERS)
Russia has spent years producing and upgrading Iranian-designed Shahed drones for use in its war against Ukraine.
During the almost five years of war in Ukraine, Russian engineers have gained extensive experience in improving their performance and adapting them to evade air defenses.
Ukrainian President Zelensky and other Officials have warned that technological improvements developed during the Ukraine war could now benefit Iran, potentially making its drones more difficult to intercept.

items.title: Google Teases Synaptics Edge AI Chip, Cuts Power 40% [2026] - shattered.io
items.summary: Google Teases Synaptics Edge AI Chip, Cuts Power 40% [2026]  shattered.io
items.content:
Google Teases Synaptics Edge AI Chip, Cuts Power 40% [2026]
Google used its annual Research@ event in Mountain View, California, on October 14, 2026, to preview a new low-power AI chip built with Synaptics, setting up a formal unveiling at Synaptics' Tech Day in San Jose on October 20. The chip pairs Google's Coral NPU M2 with Synaptics' Torq NPU and Arm CPU cores, and the companies say it cuts energy use by 40% compared with existing edge AI processors. Synaptics CEO Rahul Patel said the chip will not stay confined to lab demos. According to a report from R&D World , Patel told attendees it will also be built into Google devices, though neither company named which products or when they would ship.
The preview lands at a moment when chipmakers are racing to put AI inference directly on wearables, smart glasses, and industrial sensors instead of routing every request to the cloud. Google and Synaptics are betting that sub-6-milliwatt inference, paired with an open compiler stack, can pull developers away from the proprietary microcontroller software they have relied on for years. The timing also puts pressure on rivals already shipping edge AI silicon at scale, from Qualcomm's Snapdragon line to smaller microcontroller specialists like Ambiq, NXP, and STMicroelectronics.

Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions.
Google Research's Research@ event is the company's internal showcase for work still moving from lab to product, and this year's edition gave Synaptics a stage to describe a chip that had been in development for roughly 18 to 24 months. The device belongs to Synaptics' Astra line of AI-native processors and microcontrollers, a product family the company has built specifically for local, low-power AI workloads rather than general-purpose computing.
Patel used the Mountain View appearance to lay out the chip's capabilities without disclosing full specifications, a sequencing choice that let Google tie the story to its broader research narrative before Synaptics controls the commercial unveiling six days later. The chip can process voice, vision, motion, and contextual sensing data simultaneously, and it adds GPU and multimedia processing along with hardware-rooted security, according to the companies' public statements cited in a report from SBS .
The headline number from the preview is a claimed 40% cut in energy use for Google's Coral NPU M2, the successor to the Coral neural processing unit Google introduced the prior year. Reporting tied to the announcement, including coverage from ChosunBiz , describes M2 running on-device inference at an average power draw of less than 6 milliwatts. Neither Google nor Synaptics has specified the exact workloads used for that comparison, or which prior-generation processor served as the baseline, so the 40% figure should be read as a vendor claim rather than an independently benchmarked result.
That caveat matters because power-efficiency claims in the chip industry are notoriously workload-dependent. A processor that looks dramatically more efficient on a simple keyword-spotting task can lose much of its edge on continuous multimodal sensing, which is exactly the use case Google and Synaptics are targeting. Until Synaptics publishes a full datasheet, outside engineers will not be able to verify the 40% number against a defined test suite.
Reported efficiency claim: 40% less energy vs. prior-generation processors
Comparison baseline disclosed: No (workload and reference chip not specified)
Synaptics did not simply license Google's silicon design and ship it unchanged. The Astra chip combines the Coral NPU M2 with Synaptics' own Torq NPU and standard Arm CPU cores, giving the company a path to differentiate on top of Google's open accelerator work. That architecture lets Synaptics target a wide span of constrained devices, from battery-powered wearables to fixed industrial cameras, with one underlying platform rather than a separate chip for each category.
A less flashy but arguably more consequential part of the announcement is software. Synaptics and Google Research spent roughly 18 months building an open-source compiler on top of MLIR, the Multi-Level Intermediate Representation framework, so the chip can run standard machine learning frameworks and model formats rather than locking developers into a proprietary toolchain. Patel framed this as a break from the walled-garden software that has defined microcontroller development for years, a point echoed in R&D World's account of his remarks. Developers can already prototype against the underlying Coral NPU using Coralboard, a development platform Synaptics launched earlier this year that pairs the NPU with Astra processors ahead of the full chip's release.
Coral's first milestone was a front end built on RISC-V, the open instruction set architecture that has gained ground across the chip industry as an alternative to proprietary cores. M2 marks the second milestone and adds what Google describes as the first Coral vector processor. Google Research has also said its next design, M3, is already complete and adds native 32-bit floating-point support so the chip can run Gemma 3 270M, a compact 270-million-parameter language model, directly on-device. Neither company has given a shipping date for M3-based silicon, which means the chip debuting this month is already one generation behind Google's internal roadmap.
Rahul Patel's Pitch: From Lab Bench to Google Hardware
Patel's most direct claim from the Research@ appearance was that the chip will not stay in the lab and will also be built into Google devices, a statement widely picked up across outlets covering the preview. He also highlighted the microcontroller's support for high-density DRAM, describing memory capacity as a source of scalability for future products built on the same platform. Synaptics plans to formally unveil the chip at its Tech Day event on October 20 at 1151 McKay Drive in San Jose, which the company has billed as including a noon press and analyst briefing followed by a demonstration showcase.
What Patel did not say is just as notable. He declined to identify which Google hardware lines would adopt the chip or offer any release window, leaving a gap between the marketing claim and a verifiable product commitment. That gap is where skepticism from hardware analysts tends to concentrate, since chipmakers routinely tout future design wins that take years, or never materialize, to reach shelves.
Why Google Keeps Investing in Edge Silicon Partnerships
Google's data center strategy has long rested on designing its own Tensor Processing Units alongside the models that run on them, and the company is now pushing the same co-design philosophy to the edge. The logic, as described in reporting on the Research@ event, is that existing edge chips consume too much energy and respond too slowly for always-on, ambient AI experiences that keep personal data on the device instead of sending it to the cloud. A fragmented market of proprietary microcontroller designs compounds the problem by making it harder for developers to build once and deploy across multiple vendors' hardware.
That framing explains why Google chose a partnership model rather than building its own edge chip from scratch. Synaptics brings decades of microcontroller and sensor-fusion experience along with existing customer relationships in wearables and industrial equipment, while Google supplies the Coral accelerator design and compiler work it has already validated internally.
Billy Rutledge Makes the Case for Co-Designed Hardware
When Google and Synaptics first announced their collaboration on edge AI for the Internet of Things, Billy Rutledge, Director of Systems Research at Google Research, laid out why the two companies paired up in the first place. "Synaptics' embrace of open software and tools and proven AI hardware makes the Astra portfolio a natural fit for our ML core as we ramp to meet the uniquely challenging power, performance, cost, and space requirements of Edge AI devices," Rutledge said in the companies' joint statement announcing the partnership.
Rutledge closed that announcement with a line that reads differently now that the chip has reached a public preview. "We look forward to working together to bring our capabilities to the broad market," he said. Nearly two years of engineering separate that statement from this month's Research@ demonstration, which is roughly in line with the 18-to-24-month development window Patel cited for the project.
Synaptics spokesperson Patrick Mannion gave the clearest public explanation of the division of labor between Google's open core and Synaptics' own hardware in remarks made around CES 2025. "What we're doing is taking their open ML core and adding our own hardware engine as an enhancement," Mannion said. He added that the goal was tuning that shared foundation for the specific operators Synaptics' engine supports: "We're making that open core run better for the set of operators that we support in the engine."
Mannion also confirmed the architectural lineage underpinning the whole platform in a brief, direct answer about the subsystem's design. "It's RISC-V-based," he said, a detail that lines up with Google's own description of Coral's first milestone as a RISC-V front end before M2 added the vector processor on top of it.
Target Devices: Wearables, Smart Glasses, and the Industrial Floor
The use cases Google and Synaptics are chasing span two very different markets. On the consumer side, smart glasses, watches, and connected cameras need to recognize speech, gestures, and context without draining a small battery in a few hours. On the industrial side, vision and voice systems on factory floors need similar always-on sensing but with tighter requirements around reliability and hardware-rooted security, since these devices often sit on networks that also touch safety-critical equipment.
Covering both markets with one chip platform is an ambitious bet. It means Synaptics has to hit aggressive power targets for battery-powered wearables while also meeting the durability and security expectations of industrial buyers, all on the same underlying silicon. If the company pulls it off, Astra could become a default reference design that OEMs reach for instead of commissioning custom edge AI silicon.
This announcement did not come out of nowhere. Google's interest in specialized AI silicon traces back to a 2017 Google research paper on its first-generation Tensor Processing Unit, which reported performance-per-watt gains of 30 to 80 times over the Intel Haswell CPUs and Nvidia K80 GPUs it was benchmarked against in production neural-network inference workloads, per R&D World's account of the comparison. That data-center work eventually fed into Google's push toward edge-specific silicon, starting with early Coral development boards and continuing through a 2023 partnership with Qualcomm on a RISC-V wearable platform for Wear OS.
The Synaptics collaboration builds directly on that foundation. Google and Synaptics announced their partnership in January 2025, Synaptics launched the Coralboard development platform earlier in 2026, and the companies previewed the resulting Astra chip at Research@ this October, ahead of the formal Tech Day unveiling.
2017 Google publishes first-generation TPU research paper citing 30-80x performance-per-watt gains
2023 Google and Qualcomm announce a RISC-V wearable platform for Wear OS
January 2025 Google Research and Synaptics publicly announce their edge AI collaboration
Early 2026 Synaptics launches Coralboard, pairing the Coral NPU with Astra processors for developers
October 14, 2026 Google previews the Coral NPU M2-based Astra chip at Research@ in Mountain View
October 20, 2026 Synaptics plans a formal unveiling at Tech Day in San Jose
Competitive Landscape: Astra vs. Qualcomm, Ambiq, NXP, and STMicroelectronics
Synaptics is not entering an empty market. Qualcomm remains the volume leader in AI-capable edge silicon, having shipped more than 800 million AI-capable chips in 2025 according to industry data compiled by Axis Intelligence, with Snapdragon platforms using Hexagon NPUs rated at up to 45 TOPS for on-device inference. That positions Qualcomm at the high-performance end of the market, aimed at smartphones and premium wearables that can absorb more power draw than the ultra-constrained devices Synaptics is targeting.
Ambiq, NXP, and STMicroelectronics compete in a different tier, focused on ultra-low-power microcontrollers, embedded processing, and sensor-heavy industrial and automotive applications. Synaptics is trying to carve out space between these two groups, pitching Astra as a highly integrated, ultra-low-power platform that can still handle the multimodal sensing workloads usually reserved for higher-power chips like Qualcomm's.
Company Primary Edge AI Platform Notable Metric Market Position
Synaptics Astra (Coral NPU M2 + Torq NPU + Arm cores) Claimed <6mW inference, 40% less energy Ultra-low-power multimodal sensing
Qualcomm Snapdragon (Hexagon NPU) Up to 45 TOPS, 800M+ AI-capable chips shipped in 2025 High-performance mobile and wearable AI
Ambiq Apollo microcontroller line Ultra-low-power MCU focus Battery-constrained sensor devices
NXP i.MX / eIQ embedded processors Broad embedded and automotive portfolio Industrial and automotive edge processing
STMicroelectronics STM32 microcontrollers with AI extensions Established industrial sensor base Industrial and automotive sensor fusion
The timing of Google and Synaptics' preview lines up with a market that analysts expect to grow quickly. Grand View Research estimates, cited in Axis Intelligence's 2026 edge AI statistics roundup, value the edge AI chip market at $27.3 billion in 2025, growing to $36.2 billion in 2026. The same estimate projects the market reaching $291.8 billion by 2033, implying a compound annual growth rate of roughly 34.7%. Those figures cover the full edge AI chip category, not Synaptics or Google specifically, but they explain why a company like Synaptics is willing to spend nearly two years co-engineering silicon with a software giant rather than going it alone.
2025 $27.3 billion Grand View Research, via Axis Intelligence
2026 $36.2 billion (projected) Grand View Research, via Axis Intelligence
2033 $291.8 billion (projected) Grand View Research, via Axis Intelligence
2025-2033 CAGR Approximately 34.7% Grand View Research, via Axis Intelligence
If that growth curve holds, the edge AI chip market would more than triple in size between now and the end of the decade. That kind of expansion tends to pull in more entrants, not fewer, which raises the odds that Synaptics will face new ultra-low-power competitors within the next two or three product cycles rather than a stable five-company field.
For a chip generating this much coverage, the list of unconfirmed details is long. Neither company has disclosed the transistor count, the manufacturing process node, total on-chip memory capacity, a full-chip TOPS rating, the complete list of supported model architectures, pricing, expected production volume, or the first Google device that will actually ship with the chip inside it. The 40% power claim and the sub-6-milliwatt inference figure are the only hard performance numbers in circulation, and both come without a disclosed testing methodology.
That gap between marketing narrative and verifiable specification is normal for a pre-launch teaser, but it means most of the real analysis has to wait for October 20. Readers and investors treating this preview as a finished product announcement are getting ahead of what Google and Synaptics have actually confirmed.
Synaptics' Tech Day event in San Jose is where the preview either turns into a credible product or stalls as another unfulfilled chip tease. The company has described a noon press and analyst briefing followed by a demonstration showcase, which suggests working silicon will be on hand rather than simulations or reference designs alone. Analysts will be watching for a full TOPS rating covering the whole chip, confirmed pricing and sampling timelines for OEMs, and ideally a named lead customer or product category beyond the general "Google devices" language Patel used at Research@.
The compiler story also deserves scrutiny at the event. An open, MLIR-based toolchain is only as useful as its documentation and the breadth of model formats it actually supports on day one. If Synaptics ships the chip with a thin software stack and tells developers to wait for tooling updates, the open-compiler pitch will ring hollow regardless of how efficient the underlying silicon turns out to be.
Synaptics will likely disclose a full-chip TOPS rating and manufacturing process node at Tech Day on October 20, since withholding both details through a second public appearance would undercut the credibility of the power-efficiency claims.
Google will probably stay vague about which of its own devices will use the chip for at least one more product cycle, consistent with Patel's refusal to name specific hardware at Research@.
Qualcomm, NXP, or STMicroelectronics are likely to respond with their own ultra-low-power NPU announcements within the next two to three quarters, given how directly Synaptics is positioning Astra against the gap between their product tiers.
The open MLIR compiler approach could pressure other microcontroller vendors to loosen their proprietary software ecosystems, a shift that would play out gradually over 2027 rather than immediately.
If Grand View Research's $36.2 billion 2026 market estimate for edge AI chips proves accurate, expect more detailed Astra revenue guidance to show up in Synaptics' next earnings commentary rather than in marketing materials.
It is a low-power AI processor co-designed by Synaptics and Google Research, combining Google's Coral NPU M2 with Synaptics' own Torq NPU and Arm CPU cores. It belongs to Synaptics' Astra line of AI-native processors and microcontrollers.
When was the chip previewed and when is the full launch?
Google previewed the chip at its Research@ event in Mountain View on October 14, 2026. Synaptics plans to formally unveil it at its Tech Day event in San Jose on October 20, 2026.
Synaptics and Google say the Coral NPU M2 uses 40% less energy than existing processors and can run on-device inference at an average draw of less than 6 milliwatts. Neither company has disclosed the specific baseline chip or workload used for that comparison.
Synaptics CEO Rahul Patel said the chip will be built into Google devices, but neither company has named specific products or given a shipping timeline.
Target applications include wearables, smart glasses, connected cameras, and industrial vision and voice systems, which is any device where cloud-dependent AI processing adds too much latency or drains too much battery.
Qualcomm's Snapdragon platforms use Hexagon NPUs rated at up to 45 TOPS and shipped in more than 800 million AI-capable chips in 2025, targeting higher-power smartphones and premium wearables. Here are the 3 big things we're watching in the stock market this week
The market has been hard to please so far this earnings season. The week ahead will bring plenty of chances to flip the script. Netflix , Tesla and Club names Meta Platforms and Capital One are among the companies set to report quarterly results in the coming days, as third-quarter earnings season kicks into high gear. There aren't any huge economic reports on the docket either, brightening the spotlight on the stream of earnings updates. There may be little margin for error, if the frosty reception to last week's bank earnings are any indication. Top and bottom-line beats from the likes of Goldman Sachs were met with selling . Those with more apparent blemishes, such as State Street and Bank of America , got hit even harder . We can't say we're surprised. Jim Cramer said in early October that rising bond yields and a Federal Reserve determined to bring down inflation created "a much more difficult backdrop" for this earnings season. What's happened since Jim's warning? Tensions in the Middle East worsened , two September inflation reports came in hotter than expected , and the durability of the AI spending boom has been called further into question. The midterms are also now about two weeks away, injecting more uncertainty into the market. In other words, the backdrop hasn't gotten any easier. Now let's take a closer look at what we're expecting from Capital One, Meta and a few non-portfolio stocks with implications for our names. 1. Capital One earnings: The credit-card issuer starts us off Tuesday night. In the wake of last week's hot inflation readings, CEO Richard Fairbank's commentary on spending dynamics across income cohorts will be especially notable. As for the numbers, net interest income came up short last quarter due to thinner-than-expected net interest margin, so we'll be looking for sequential expansion this time around. Net charge-offs — the amount Capital One assumes it won't be able to recover from borrowers — were also a bit high in July, so we want to see better performance there. Better charge-offs, along with a release on loan reserves — the amount the bank sets aside in anticipation of bad loans — would help instill greater confidence in the quality of the credit the firm has extended. Given what we heard last week from the banks, we do expect credit commentary to be neutral to positive. Capital One's non-interest expenses will be under the microscope. The company has been investing heavily into the business, which has held back earnings in recent quarters and, in turn, the stock. But, at less than 9 times forward earnings, Capital One shares look too cheap to give up on. We also hope to see more tangible benefits from the Discover acquisition, though we recognize full expense synergies are not expected to be achieved until the middle of next year. As of Friday, Capital One is expected to report earnings of $5.50 per share on revenue of $16.26 billion, according to estimates compiled by LSEG. 2. Meta earnings: The Facebook and Instagram parent reports after Wednesday's close, and it is sure to be an exciting earnings call. CEO Mark Zuckerberg is riding high from the viral launch of its agentic AI platform assistant, Muse. While directional commentary on adoption trends figures to be positive, we're interested to see if management shares actual numbers, both in terms of overall engagement (like daily active users) and the breakdown of user types (such as paid versus free). Against the engagement commentary, we must acknowledge that this positive reception will embolden Zuckerberg to press the bet and keep investing aggressively in compute infrastructure. As a result, commentary on AI spending intentions — and how it will be funded — are going to counterbalance the Muse optimism as analysts put pen to paper. How well Zuckerberg and CFO Susan Li are able to explain and justify the spending is sure to impact the stock market reaction. Will they point to current monetization trends, or detail the future revenue potential? Outside of Muse, the focus will be on the company's core Family of Apps business, and whether it's benefiting from the more advanced AI models coming out of Meta Superintelligence Labs. Meta is expected to report earnings per share of $5.94 on revenue of $63.32 billion, according to LSEG, as of Friday. 3. Non-Club reports to watch: Capital One and Meta aren't the only earnings releases on our radar. While it is impossible to cover every name (though we still have to try), there are several companies reporting that every investor should monitor. We'll group them into thematic buckets: AI buildout: Alongside Meta on Wednesday night, we'll hear from Lam Research and Texas Instruments . Lam Research is a capital equipment manufacturer, meaning it makes equipment that chipmakers need to manufacture semiconductors (both logic and memory chips), so it offers a window into efforts to close the supply-demand imbalance. Though Texas Instruments makes semiconductors used across a bunch of industries, its fast-growing business selling power management chips into data centers is what we care about most. On Thursday night, Western Digital reports. The hard-drive maker sits within the broader storage and memory complex alongside Club name Micron (though they make different things). Still, the market reaction to Western Digital's numbers will be a good temperature check. Aerospace and defense: There's a bunch of companies reporting across this industry, with implications for Club name Boeing . On Tuesday, Pratt & Whitney owner RTX, engine maker GE Aerospace , and defense giant Northrop Grumman all report. The big Navy fighter jet contract that Boeing recently won may come up on Northrop's conference call because some thought the company was the favorite to secure it. Throughout the week, we'll also hear from key Boeing customers in United Airlines, Alaska Air, Southwest Airlines and American Airlines. Consumer spending read-throughs: We'll also listen to what the airlines are saying about the health of the consumer in the face of rising gas prices and inflation. In the same vein, General Motors, Tesla, Netflix, Spotify, Procter & Gamble, and American Express all report. items.content:
Top analysts are bullish on the growth potential of these 3 stocks
A cyclist rides past the Meta sign outside the headquarters of Facebook parent company Meta Platforms in Mountain View, California, on Nov. 9, 2022.
Fears around the artificial intelligence trade and higher pressure on oil prices are weighing on global markets, but a few stocks offer investors solid growth prospects even in choppy times.
Investors with a long-term horizon can look beyond the ongoing volatility and track the recommendations of top Wall Street analysts to pick attractive stocks with strong long-term growth potential.
Here are three stocks favored by some of Wall Street's top pros, according to TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.
Health insurer UnitedHealth delivered better-than-expected results for the third quarter of 2026. The company also raised its full-year earnings outlook, reflecting continued progress on its turnaround plan.
Following the Q3 print, Morgan Stanley analyst Erin Wright reiterated a buy rating on UNH stock with a price target of $529 . " UNH 's beat & raise reinforces turnaround momentum, with improving MA [Medicare Advantage]/Optum Health supporting a higher '26 EPS baseline & upside to '27 consensus," said Wright.
The five-star analyst added that better-than-expected performance in the UnitedHealthcare and Optum Health businesses supported another upgrade to the company's 2026 adjusted earnings per share outlook to at least $20.50. Wright noted that UNH raised the earnings guidance despite incremental investments planned for the fourth quarter of 2026.
Furthermore, Wright highlighted management's view that the consensus 2027 EPS of $22.63 was too conservative. Reaching even the low end of the company's 13% to 16% long-term EPS growth target would imply an EPS of $23.17.
Wright raised her 2026 EPS estimate to $20.65 from $19.82 and 2027 EPS to $23.24 from $22.54, reflecting the latest upside and an improving 2026 medical loss ratio to 87.4% from 88.1%. Overall, she believes that UNH's operational performance continues to improve, increasing her confidence in its UHC strategy and Optum Health turnaround execution.
Wright ranks No. 264 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. Her ratings have been successful 64% of the time, delivering an average return of 15%.  See UnitedHealth Ownership Structure on TipRanks.
Social media giant Meta Platforms has been making headlines since the launch of its Muse AI agent, which is seeing solid traction . Investors look forward to updates on the company's AI strategy when it announces its third-quarter results on Oct. 21.
Heading into Q3 earnings, Guggenheim analyst Michael Morris maintained a buy rating on Meta stock and increased his price target to $850 from $700, reflecting higher estimates for 2027. He expects Muse usage momentum and engagement levels to shape investor sentiment into the Q3 earnings call.
Specifically, Morris highlighted that, according to Apptopia, Muse reached 1.3 million daily active users in five weeks versus 300,000 in the first week. Given that Muse's current adoption represents less than 0.05% of Meta's 3.6 billion daily active user base, the analyst expects management to prioritize boosting usage over near-term monetization.
"Over time, we believe Muse monetizes primarily through businesses paying to reach consumers through their agents, consistent with the economics of Meta's core advertising business, rather than consumer wallets," said the five-star analyst. He added that the checkout integrations with Shopify and PayPal reflect this framework.
While there are concerns that a rival could overtake Muse or the recently launched Muse Wonder and push Meta into a prolonged cycle of overinvestment, Morris remains bullish due to the company's strong record in scaling WhatsApp and competing strongly with TikTok via Reels as well as free distribution to an extensive user base.
Morris ranks No. 629 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been successful 57% of the time, delivering an average return of 13.2%.  See Meta Platforms KPIs on TipRanks.
Next is semiconductor company Marvell Technology . Earlier this month, Marvell held its Investor Day, where it raised its total addressable market estimate to $400 billion by 2030, reflecting solid AI-led demand tailwinds.
After hosting a non-deal roadshow with Marvell 's senior management following the Investor Day, Stifel analyst Tore Svanberg reiterated a buy rating on the stock with a price target of $370 .
The five-star analyst said that a major focus of the roadshow was the XPU and XPU Attach mix, as Marvell's Custom business expands toward its FY31 revenue target of $30 billion. In this regard, management reiterated that it expects a balanced mix of XPU and XPU Attach revenue in FY31, though it noted that either segment could grow rapidly enough to shift the mix toward 60/40 or 40/60.
While XPU drove most of the nearly $1.5 billion Custom revenue in FY26, Svanberg expects Marvell's XPU Attach business to grow substantially through the end of the decade, leading to a more balanced mix in this business. At the Investor Day event, the company raised its FY29 Custom target from more than $10 billion to over $12 billion, mainly driven by strength in the XPU Attach business.
Svanberg said that another key topic in the roadshow was whether Marvell can secure enough capacity to meet its raised targets. Management said that it met with suppliers ahead of Investor Day to share its five-year goals and received commitments to support these targets. The analyst believes that Marvell's supply chain commitments give it a competitive edge over rivals as customers seek reliable partners for large-scale infrastructure buildouts.
Svanberg ranks No. 91 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 58% of the time, delivering an average return of 31.8%.  See Marvell Technology Statistics on TipRanks.

items.title: Photos show luxury boat with 50m pool and water slides near Kim Jong Un's summer retreat
items.summary: Satellite images give clues about how Kim spends his holidays - something far out of reach for most North Koreans.
items.content:
By Soram Cheon ,Â  BBC Korean Â  and Â  Aghnia Adzkia ,Â  East Asia Visual Journalism
An 80m (263ft) luxury vessel has been repeatedly spotted in satellite images off North Korea's Wonsan coast from July to mid-October this year.
What stands out is the 50m swimming pool along the deck, with a cluster of waterslides at one end.
After sitting idle for months at a maintenance facility, it relocated in early July to waters off a strip of coastline known as the Kalma Peninsula.
This is close to Wonsan, a seaside resort with a sprawling villa used by North Korean leader Kim Jong Un and his family.
It was not the only large vessel on the move. A handful of others were also repeatedly seen near Kim's villa, in satellite images analysed by the BBC.
The vessels are widely believed to be used by Kim and his family. Former North Korean officials, defectors and experts say it would be difficult for anyone unconnected to the regime's leadership to own or freely use vessels of this size.
"In winter, they would keep them at the shipyard. When summer came, they would bring them out and move them to Kim Jong Un's villa or towards Kalma, and use them for swimming and recreation," says Ri Jong Ho.
Ri was once an official at the Workers' Party's Office 39, which is believed to be involved in raising and managing foreign currency for the leadership.
The wealth of those who sit at the top of the secretive North Korean dictatorship is just as hard to pin down as the country's economic figures.
The United Nations and others rely on estimates to classify North Korea as one of the world's poorest countries, with an especially large military budget that funds a sanctioned nuclear programme.
Most North Koreans, according to a 2025 UN report, live under "systematic, widespread and gross human rights violations" with total state control, widespread forced labour and chronic food shortages that leave an estimated 40% of the population undernourished.
But the regime has long been known to live in luxury.
We don't know the cost of the vessels seen in the satellite imagery, but comparable luxury yachts run from tens of millions to over $100m (Â£75m). Kim's much smaller, 29-metre Princess yacht was previously estimated to be worth about $7m.
While vessel locations alone cannot definitively establish the family's whereabouts, their movements - which overlap with gaps in Kim's public appearances - point to activities that would otherwise remain out of public view.
Wonsan is where Kim Jong Un spent part of his childhood with his mother, according to biographers and intelligence reports, and one expert told the BBC the city has been associated with the family since his father Kim Jong Il's rule.
A defector who served for 13 years guarding residences used by then leader Kim Jong Il - through the 1990s to the early 2000s - told the BBC the villas around Wonsan were used as a retreat by the elite. He recalls seeing dozens of children and teens waterskiing during summer.
North Korean state media rarely publishes reports about Kim being on holiday, instead framing such visits as official inspections or guidance. But defectors interviewed by the BBC appeared to be aware that the family spent holidays in Wonsan, suggesting that at least some North Koreans knew about it.
North Korean state media also claims Wonsan is home to high-rise hotels, restaurants, shops, sports facilities and water parks, and can accommodate nearly 20,000 visitors.
State media and Russian outlets have published images of small groups of Russian tourists visiting the Wonsan Kalma resort, which opened in July 2025. Although developed to attract foreign visitors, the resort is also open to local tourists.
Image caption, North Korean tourists on a beach in Kalma
A South Korean news report, citing an unnamed source, says some locals were offered four-night tour packages for around $100, a substantial sum for most North Koreans. The country's per capita GDP - around $667 in 2024, according to the UN - is a small fraction of South Korea's $36,227.
For the majority of North Koreans, holidays are out of reach. And while a growing middle class does exist, they might not have much time for leisure.
Defectors told the BBC that workers, office employees and cooperative farmers are legally entitled to 14 days of annual leave, but this is rarely followed.
Taking consecutive days off to travel is unusual. People typically take weekend trips or travel during national holidays instead of designated "summer holidays".
Even if leave is granted, travel itself is restricted, with official permission required for people to travel outside their city or county. Moving freely is sometimes as much a luxury as the holiday itself.
Image caption, Ordinary North Koreans struggle to earn a decent living
The BBC tracked four large vessels around Wonsan, measuring approximately 50m, 55m, 60m and 80m. All four vessels repeatedly appeared around Kim's Wonsan villa this year.
The largest vessel showed the clearest activity, moving from the dock to the waters off the Kalma Peninsula, where it has been since July.
Two of the other vessels - 50m and 55m - were repeatedly seen until the end of August around Tae and Sin islands, close to Wonsan.
Satellite images also showed four smaller boats alongside the 50m vessel.
Image caption, The 50m vessel was seen in waters near Tae island on 4 July 2026.
Satellite imagery expert Jeong Seong-hak said the smaller boats ferried people, fuel and supplies to the larger vessel, adding that small islands like Tae and Sin offered "secluded maritime retreats where privacy can be maintained away from public view".
The 60m vessel was repeatedly seen near Kim's Wonsan villa until as recently as last week.
Though North Korea has never publicly disclosed the vessels' official ownership, BBC's analysis of historical satellite imagery found a large vessel with the same distinctive characteristics in Wonsan in 2002, when Kim Jong Il ruled North Korea.
Former NBA star Dennis Rodman, who visited the North in 2013, told the Sun that he had spent much of his seven-day visit with Kim Jong Un around Wonsan, where they went jet-skiing and horse riding.
He also described a 60m vessel they used as a cross between a ferry and a Disney boat. It is unclear if this is the same 60m boat pictured in the above satellite imagery.
To most North Koreans, the life lived by the Kims and others who support the regime would seem not just extravagant but unimaginable. Especially because state propaganda is dedicated to presenting the "supreme leader" as a selfless man who always puts the nation first.
"Kim Jong Un is supposed to be a 'leader of the people'," Ri Jong Ho says, "yet he has four luxury vessels like these while ordinary people are struggling just to get one meal a day."
